items.statement: Assume the following: S = Spec A with A an artinian ring; X̄ is proper over S; D = X̄ \ X is locally principal, with ideal I (the image of O_X̄(−D) → O_X̄); and F̄ is a coherent sheaf on X̄ with F = F̄|_X. Then H^i(X̄, j_!F) ≅ lim_n H^i(X̄, I^n F̄) for all i. This is Hartshorne's definition of coherent cohomology with compact supports [Har72] (Remark 2.3.6).
items.note: Proposition 2.3.5 (p. 16) is planned nowhere, and no layer plans Hartshorne's coherent cohomology with compact support [Har72]. The proof uses: the stabilisation M[f^n] = M[f^{n+1}] for a finite module over a noetherian ring (ascending chain condition, in Mathlib); finiteness of H^i(X̄, I^nF̄) over the artinian ring A for proper X̄, which JacobianChallenge Layer B plans over a field ('finite-dimensionality for proper X/k') and AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:A0-extension extends beyond curves; and the Mittag-Leffler argument, whose EGA 0_III 13.2.3 form PAPER-PILLONI-20 records as planned in DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra:P7. The page prints H^i(X, j_!F); X̄ is meant.

items.name: j_* as the colimit of the twists F̄(nD)
items.statement: Let j : X → X̄ be an open immersion with locally principal complement D, given by O_X̄(−D) → O_X̄ as in §2.3.1. Let F ∈ D(O_{X,■}) and F̄ ∈ D(O_{X̄,■}) with j^*F̄ = F. If F̄ is discrete, there is a canonical isomorphism j_*F ≅ colim_n F̄(nD) in D(O_{X̄,■}), the colimit being along the maps F̄(nD) → F̄((n+1)D) induced by O_X̄(−D) → O_X̄.
items.note: Proposition 2.3.8 (p. 16) is planned nowhere. For a discrete (quasi-coherent) F̄ it is the classical description of j_*j^*F̄ by sections with poles along a locally principal D, locally M ⊗_A A[1/f] = colim(M →f M →f ⋯); neither library has this for sheaves on schemes, and the solid statement needs in addition that the ordinary localisation of a discrete module is solid.

items.name: Cohomology on qcqs schemes commutes with filtered colimits
items.statement: On a quasi-compact and quasi-separated scheme, cohomology commutes with filtered colimits of quasi-coherent sheaves.
items.locator: §2.3.7, proof of Corollary 2.3.9, p. 16; §2.3.10, proof of Corollary 2.3.11, p. 17
items.note: Tau Ceti defines H^i(X, M) for O_X-modules (Scheme.Modules.Cohomology, Mathlib's Ext from the constant sheaf) with long exact and Mayer–Vietoris sequences, but neither library proves that it commutes with filtered colimits on quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes, and no atlas layer states it (tauceti ProfiniteCohomology Layer 4 plans the analogue only for profinite group cohomology). SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 ('construct sheaf cohomology, localization, proper/smooth base change and compact support') owns sheaf cohomology of schemes. In Corollary 2.3.11 (p. 17) the colimits are of non-discrete solid objects, where the needed fact is that RΓ on a qcqs scheme is computed by a finite Čech limit, which commutes with colimits in a stable category. External input: The Stacks Project [Sta22], Tag 01FF (cited in Corollary 2.3.9).

items.name: Cohomology of j_*F as a colimit of cohomology of twists
items.statement: Under the assumptions of Proposition 2.3.8, RΓ(X̄, j_*F) ≅ colim_n RΓ(X̄, F̄(nD)).
items.note: Corollary 2.3.9 (p. 16) is planned nowhere; it is Proposition 2.3.8 combined with the commutation of cohomology with filtered colimits on the quasi-compact quasi-separated X̄ (missing; Stacks Tag 01FF in the paper).

items.name: A cohomological correspondence extends to twisted sheaves on the compactification
items.statement: Let 𝒞 = (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−) be a dynamic compactification of (C, X, p1, p2), with X̄ \ X = D = D+ ∪ D− and D+, D− locally principal. Let F be a coherent sheaf on X, F̄ a coherent extension of F to X̄, and T : p2^*F → p1^!F a cohomological correspondence. Then there are n ≥ 0 and a map T : p̄2^*(F̄(−nD−)) → p̄1^!(F̄(nD+)) in D(O_{C̄,■}) whose restriction to C is T.
items.note: Proposition 2.3.13 (p. 17) is planned nowhere. The proof uses j_C^*p̄2^* = p2^*j_X^* and j_C^*p̄1^! = p1^!j_X^*, Proposition 2.3.8 on C̄ for the discrete objects p̄2^*F̄ and p̄1^!F̄, pseudo-coherence of p̄2^*F̄ to factor through a finite stage, the set-theoretic identity C̄ \ C = p̄1^*D+ ∪ p̄2^*D− (which uses the dynamic conditions), and the projection formula for p̄1^!.

items.name: Corollary 2.3.11: cohomology with partial support as limits and colimits of twisted cohomology
items.statement:
Let X ↪ X̄ be an open immersion of schemes of finite type over Spec Z with X̄ ∖ X = D = D₊ ∪ D₋, where D₊ and D₋ are locally principal closed subschemes (each is cut out by the image of a map O_X̄(−D±) → O_X̄ from an invertible sheaf). Let F̄ be a coherent sheaf on X̄ with restriction F to X, and write F̄(n₊D₊ − n₋D₋) := F̄ ⊗ O_X̄(−D₊)^{⊗(−n₊)} ⊗ O_X̄(−D₋)^{⊗n₋}. Then, in the solid derived category,
RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F) = colim_{n₊≥0} lim_{n₋≥0} RΓ(X̄, F̄(n₊D₊ − n₋D₋)),
RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F) = lim_{n₋≥0} colim_{n₊≥0} RΓ(X̄, F̄(n₊D₊ − n₋D₋)).
Here RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄,F) = RΓ(X̄, (j₊)_*(j₋)_!F) for X ↪ X̄∖D₊ ↪ X̄, and RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄,F) = RΓ(X̄, (i₋)_!(i₊)_*F) for X ↪ X̄∖D₋ ↪ X̄ (Definition 2.2.4).
items.note: Neither library has it and no atlas layer plans it. Mathlib and Tau Ceti have none of the following: the solid derived category D(O_{X̄,■}), extension by zero j_! of quasi-coherent sheaves along an open immersion, or cohomology with partial support RΓ_{D₊,D₋}, RΓ_{D₋,D₊} (Definition 2.2.4). The proof (p. 17) combines Proposition 2.3.2 (j_*j^*F̄ = colim_n F̄(nD) and, for pseudo-coherent F̄, j_!F = lim_n F̄(−nD)) with the fact that in the solid setting RΓ commutes with limits and colimits on quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes. The solid quasi-coherent six functors are targets only of AnalyticStacks AS.3 ('Solid quasi-coherent sheaves (Scholze Lecture IX)'), a draft roadmap that is not in the atlas. Cohomology with partial support on a dynamic compactification is the basic object of the paper's §2 formalism.

items.name: Corollary 2.3.14: T_C is the limit–colimit of maps between twisted cohomologies
items.statement:
Assume the situation of Proposition 2.3.13, and suppose we are given maps α₊: p̄₂*O_X̄(D₊) → p̄₁*O_X̄(D₊) and α₋: p̄₂*O_X̄(−D₋) → p̄₁*O_X̄(−D₋). Assume they are compatible with the canonical maps s₊: O_X̄ → O_X̄(D₊) and t₋: O_X̄(−D₋) → O_X̄, that is, α₊ ∘ p̄₂*(s₊) = p̄₁*(s₊) and p̄₁*(t₋) ∘ α₋ = p̄₂*(t₋). This holds, for instance, for the maps induced by inclusions of ideals as in Lemma 2.1.17. Let n be as in Proposition 2.3.13. For all k₊, k₋ ≥ 0, T induces maps
RΓ(X̄, F̄(−nD₋ − k₋D₋ + k₊D₊)) → RΓ(X̄, F̄(nD₊ − k₋D₋ + k₊D₊)).
Each is obtained in three steps: pull back along p̄₂; apply the map of Proposition 2.3.13 twisted by α₊^{⊗k₊} ⊗ α₋^{⊗k₋}: p̄₂*O_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) → p̄₁*O_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) (using the projection formula); take the trace along the proper map p̄₁. These maps are compatible with the transition maps in k₊ and in k₋. After passing to the limit over k₋ and the colimit over k₊ as in Corollary 2.3.11, they induce the endomorphism T_C of RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F) and of RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F) constructed in Proposition 2.2.10.
items.note: Missing for the same reasons as Proposition 2.3.13, on which it rests. The proof (p. 17) twists the extended correspondence of Proposition 2.3.13 by the given maps p̄₂*O_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) → p̄₁*O_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋). This writes T_C of Proposition 2.2.10 as a limit–colimit of maps between cohomologies of coherent sheaves on X̄, the form in which Lemma 2.4.4 is applied. The paper does not state the compatibility of the given maps with the canonical maps O_X̄ → O_X̄(D₊) and O_X̄(−D₋) → O_X̄, which the statement above includes, but it tacitly assumes it (sourceIssues E25). As printed, Corollary 2.3.14 only assumes that some maps p̄₂*O_X̄(D₊) → p̄₁*O_X̄(D₊) and p̄₂*O_X̄(−D₋) → p̄₁*O_X̄(−D₋) are given.

items.name: An operator on a solid complex as a module over (A[T], A)■ (§2.4.1)
items.statement: Let A be a finitely generated Z-algebra and M ∈ D(A■) with an endomorphism T. Then M is regarded as an object of D((A[T],A)■), the derived category of modules over the analytic ring A[T] with the solid structure induced from A (equivalently, A[T]-modules in D(A■)). To do this, replace M by the quasi-isomorphic two-term complex M ⊗_A A[X] →^{X−T} M ⊗_A A[X] (degrees −1 and 0), where X is a new variable that is afterwards renamed T. The map X − T is injective with cokernel M, on which X acts by T. Footnote 2 of the paper: this replacement is unique only up to a non-unique isomorphism, and an ∞-categorical treatment might be desirable.
items.note: No atlas layer has the relative analytic ring (A[T],A)■, that is A[T] with the measures induced from A■ ([CSb], appendix to Lecture VIII). VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS2 plans solid modules over finitely generated Z-algebras but no relative structures. The relative structures are targets only of the draft SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 ('D(Z[T]■) as a localisation of D((Z[T],Z)■)'; discrete Huber pairs '(A,S)■'), which is not in the atlas. Mathlib has only the predicate CondensedMod.IsSolid. The printed replacement (p. 18) is 'cone(M ⊗_A A[X] →^{X−T} M ⊗_A A[X])[1]'. With the usual convention for mapping cones it is the unshifted cone, with terms in degrees −1 and 0, that is quasi-isomorphic to M, and the statement is written that way. Footnote 2 (p. 18): 'This replacement is only unique up to a non unique isomorphism, an ∞-categorical treatment might be desirable here.' A formalisation therefore needs the A[T]-module structure to be built functorially rather than by this choice.

items.name: Definition 2.4.2: ordinary part M^ord
items.statement:
For M ∈ D((A[T],A)■), that is, M ∈ D(A■) with an operator T (§2.4.1), the ordinary part is
M^ord := M ⊗^L_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■ ∈ D(A[T,T⁻¹]■),
where A[T,T⁻¹]■ is the solid analytic ring structure on A[T,T⁻¹], in which both T and T⁻¹ are solid. M^ord is regarded as an object of D(A■) by restriction of scalars. T acts invertibly on it.
items.note: The atlas plans ordinary projectors only for finite and profinite modules and for perfect complexes. PadicFamilies:L0a: 'For an endomorphism U of a finite underlying module, prove the Fitting decomposition into its eventually invertible image and eventually killed kernel', and 'Apply the result degreewise to finite perfect/cohomological complexes with commuting U and differential'. IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants:IHG.2: 'Prove localization decompositions over complete coefficient rings' for Hecke actions on bounded perfect complexes. The solid definition, a base change from (A[T],A)■ to A[T,T⁻¹]■, is planned nowhere; both analytic rings are targets only of the draft SolidAnalyticRings SA.3. It generalises the ordinary part of Pilloni (2020), which was planned at L0a and IHG.2 for perfect complexes and routed by source to L0a for locally finite actions (e = lim T^{N!}, §2 there): no local-finiteness hypothesis is needed. On bounded complexes of finite modules over an artinian local ring it agrees with the projector (Lemma 2.4.3).

items.name: Vanishing of A[[T]] ⊗_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■
items.statement: For a finitely generated Z-algebra A, A[[T]] ⊗^L_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■ = 0. Hence M^ord = 0 for every M ∈ D((A[[T]],A)■), in particular for every bounded complex of finite A-modules on which T acts nilpotently.
items.locator: Used in case (1) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3, p. 18, and in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4, p. 24
items.note: The paper uses this without proof. It appears in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3(1) (p. 18) and, in the form A[T,T⁻¹]■ ⊗_{A[T]} A[[T]] = 0, in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24). The argument recorded here uses [CSb] Theorem 8.13 in the form stated in the proof of Lemma 2.4.4(1): A[[T]] = lim_n A[T]/(Tⁿ), each A[T]/(Tⁿ) is killed once T is invertible, and base change to A[T,T⁻¹]■ commutes with limits. No atlas layer plans computations in (A[T],A)■. The draft SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 has the neighbouring acceptance test 'a complete (Z[T],Z)■-module M is T-solid exactly when RHom(Z((T^{-1})),M)=0', but that roadmap is not in the atlas. External input: Not cited in the paper. It follows from Clausen–Scholze's solid formalism: A[[T]] = lim_n A[T]/(T^n), each A[T]/(T^n) becomes 0 once T is inverted, and base change to A[T,T⁻¹]■ commutes with limits ([CSb], Theorem 8.13, as used in Lemma 2.4.4(1)).

items.name: Clausen–Scholze, Theorem 8.13: relative solid analytic rings and the functors j_!, f_!, f^!
items.statement:
Let R → S → B be maps of finitely generated Z-algebras.
(i) (B,R)■, with (B,R)■[S] = R■[S] ⊗_R B, is an analytic ring.
(ii) The forgetful functor D((B,S)■) → D((B,R)■) has a left adjoint j* = − ⊗^L_{(B,R)■} (B,S)■. This in turn has a left adjoint j_!, which satisfies j_!j*M = M ⊗^L_{(B,R)■} j_!B.
(iii) For f: Spec B → Spec R, the functor f_!: D(B■) → D(R■) (j_! followed by the forgetful functor) commutes with direct sums, satisfies the projection formula f_!((M ⊗^L_{R■} B■) ⊗^L_{B■} N) ≅ M ⊗^L_{R■} f_!N, and is compatible with composition.
(iv) f_! has a right adjoint f^!. The object f^!R is discrete and a bounded-below complex of finitely generated B-modules. If f has finite Tor-dimension, f^!R is bounded and f^!M = (M ⊗^L_{R■} B■) ⊗^L_{B■} f^!R. If f is a complete intersection, f^!R is invertible.
The paper uses it in the form: the functor − ⊗^L_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■ commutes with all colimits and all limits (Lemma 2.4.4(1)). It also cites the theorem for proper base change (Lemma 2.2.2).
items.locator: Cited in the proof of Lemma 2.4.4, p. 18 (as [CSb] thm. 8.13)
items.note: Mathlib has condensed modules and the predicate CondensedMod.IsSolid, whose docstring says 'This is not the correct definition of solid R-modules for a general R'. It has nothing on analytic rings, j_!, f_! or f^!. VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS2 plans solid modules over finitely generated Z-algebras, not the relative rings (A,R)■ or the shriek functors. Two draft roadmaps, neither in the atlas, have these as targets. SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 has the relative rings: 'The pre-analytic and analytic structures (A,S)■ (Definition 5.5.4)'. AnalyticStacks AS.3 has the six functors on schemes of finite type: 'Theorem 9.7: the formalism X↦D■(X) on derived schemes almost of finite type over Z, with P proper maps, I open immersions and E separated maps'. The statement matches Theorem 8.13 in the appendix to Lecture VIII of the current Clausen–Scholze notes: '(A,R)□[S] := R□[S] ⊗_R A', parts (i)–(iv). External input: D. Clausen, P. Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics (course notes; the paper's [CSb]), Theorem 8.13 in the appendix to Lecture VIII, as numbered in the current (May 2026) version of the notes.

items.name: Lemma 2.4.3: ordinary/non-ordinary decomposition over an artinian local ring
items.statement: Let A be an artinian local ring and M a bounded complex of finite A-modules with an endomorphism T (in D(A)). Then there is a unique direct sum decomposition M = M^ord ⊕ M^nord such that T is invertible on M^ord (which is the ordinary part of Definition 2.4.2) and M^nord is an A[[T]]-module. That is, T is nilpotent on M^nord, M^nord ∈ D((A[[T]],A)■), and (M^nord)^ord = 0.
items.note: Only the decomposition part has planned or library counterparts, and only for other objects. Mathlib has the Fitting decomposition for modules, LinearMap.eventually_isCompl_ker_pow_range_pow (M = ker fⁿ ⊕ range fⁿ for n large, M noetherian and artinian). PadicFamilies:L0a plans the finite projector, and IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants:IHG.2 plans 'localization decompositions over complete coefficient rings' for Hecke actions on bounded perfect complexes. Here T is an endomorphism in D(A) of a bounded complex of finite modules, which need not be perfect. The proof (p. 18) decomposes the finite A-algebra B generated by T in End(M) into local factors B_i, with idempotents e_i and M_i = e_iM. If T ∈ m_{B_i}, then Tⁿ = 0 on M_i and M_i^ord = 0, by the vanishing of A[[T]] ⊗_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■. Otherwise M_i is discrete over A[T,T⁻¹] and M_i^ord = M_i. The identification with the solid ordinary part of Definition 2.4.2 is planned nowhere.

items.name: Lemma 2.4.4(1): the ordinary part commutes with colimits and limits
items.statement: Let M = colim_{i∈I} lim_{j∈J} M_{i,j} in D(A■), with I filtered and J cofiltered. Suppose the endomorphism T of M is induced by endomorphisms of the M_{i,j} compatible with the transition maps, so that M = colim_i lim_j M_{i,j} in D((A[T],A)■). Then M^ord = colim_{i∈I} lim_{j∈J} M_{i,j}^ord.
items.note: Missing, together with Definition 2.4.2. The proof (p. 18) regards M = colim_i lim_j M_{i,j} in D((A[T],A)■) and quotes: 'Since − ⊗_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T⁻¹]■ commutes with colim and lim by [CSb] thm. 8.13'. Relative solid rings and this exactness property are targets only of the draft roadmaps SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 and AnalyticStacks AS.3. The lemma passes the ordinary part through the limit–colimit description of cohomology with partial support (Corollaries 2.3.11 and 2.3.14).

items.name: Lemma 2.4.4(2): ordinary part of a Z≥0 × Z≥0 system with a diagonal operator T′
items.note: Missing. The printed diagrams on p. 18, checked on the page image, give conditions (a)–(c) as stated. By these conditions T is the composite of one horizontal map, one vertical map and T′, in any order that makes sense. Since T is a quasi-isomorphism on ordinary parts, all transition maps and T′ become quasi-isomorphisms, and M^ord ≅ M_{i,j}^ord (pp. 18–19). Once Definition 2.4.2 and part (1) are available, the argument is elementary. It is the mechanism behind the control statement of Proposition 2.5.4.

items.name: Lemma 2.4.4(3): ordinary decomposition of a colimit–limit of finite complexes
items.statement: In the situation of Lemma 2.4.4(1), assume that A is artinian and that each M_{i,j} is a bounded complex of finite A-modules. Then M = M^ord ⊕ M^nord, where M^nord is an A[[T]]-module (so (M^nord)^ord = 0).
items.note: Missing. The printed proof is 'The last point follows from lemma 2.4.3' (p. 19). Three facts are used. The decompositions of the M_{i,j} are compatible with the transition maps, by the uniqueness in Lemma 2.4.3. An artinian A is a finite product of artinian local rings, whereas Lemma 2.4.3 assumes A local. A[[T]]-modules are stable under the limits and colimits taken.

items.name: Definition 2.4.5: map of finite rank
items.statement: Let M, N ∈ D(A■). A map T: M → N has finite rank if it factors as M → C → N, where C is a complex whose cohomology groups are finite A-modules.
items.note: Planned nowhere. The atlas plans compact operators only for Banach modules: LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L4, 'nuclear/Fredholm determinants in the precise compact-operator setting, slope decompositions', used by PadicFamilies:L2a. A map in D(A■) that factors through a complex with finite cohomology is a different notion, and it is what the higher Coleman part of the paper (§2.10) uses.

items.name: Lemma 2.4.6: the ordinary part of a finite rank endomorphism has finite cohomology
items.statement: Let A be an artinian local ring, M ∈ D(A■), and T: M → M an endomorphism of finite rank. Then M^ord ∈ D(A■) is a complex whose cohomology groups are finite A-modules.
items.note: Missing. The proof (p. 19) goes as follows. Factor T as M → C → M. The induced map M^ord → C^ord is a quasi-isomorphism because it factors T. Finally, 'Hⁱ(C^ord) is a direct factor of Hⁱ(C) by lemma 2.4.3'. Lemma 2.4.3 is stated for bounded complexes, while Definition 2.4.5 does not require C to be bounded. In the applications C is the cohomology of a coherent sheaf on a proper scheme, hence bounded.

items.name: Theorem 2.5.1(1): the two ordinary cohomologies with partial support agree
items.note: Ordinary cohomology with partial support on a strict dynamic compactification is planned nowhere. The proof is Proposition 2.5.4 (p. 20). After the normalisation of Lemma 2.5.3, both ordinary parts equal RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋))^ord for k₊, k₋ ≥ m. This is the abstract form of the higher Hida complexes that Pilloni (2020) builds by hand for GSp4 on the p-rank ≥ 1 locus (Theorems 11.2.1 and 11.3.1 there, routed to HigherHidaAndColemanTheory). Here it is stated for any correspondence with a strict dynamic compactification.

items.name: Theorem 2.5.1(2): finiteness of ordinary cohomology over an artinian base
items.statement: In the setting of Theorem 2.5.1(1), if A is artinian, then RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F)^ord ≃ RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F)^ord is represented by a bounded complex of finite A-modules.
items.note: Missing. By Proposition 2.5.4 (p. 20) the ordinary cohomology is RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋))^ord. Since X̄ is proper, that complex is a bounded complex of finite A-modules, and its ordinary part is a direct factor by Lemma 2.4.4. So the statement rests on the solid ordinary part and on finiteness of coherent cohomology of proper schemes over A.

items.name: Theorem 2.5.1(3): independence of the strict dynamic compactification
items.statement:
In the setting of Theorem 2.5.1(1), let C′ = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′₁, p̄′₂, D′₊, D′₋) → C be a map of strict dynamic compactifications of (C, X, p₁, p₂). By Definition 2.1.28 this is a map ξ of compactifications with D′₊ ⊇ ξ*D₊ and D′₋ ⊇ ξ*D₋, not necessarily a strict map. Then there are canonical quasi-isomorphisms
RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F)^ord → RΓ_{D′₊,D′₋}(X̄′, F)^ord and
RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F)^ord → RΓ_{D′₋,D′₊}(X̄′, F)^ord,
with ordinary parts taken for T_C and T_{C′} respectively.
items.note: Missing. The proof (§2.5.6, p. 20) runs as follows. By Proposition 2.2.11 and Lemma 2.1.13 it reduces to one compactification with nested divisors, the case D′₊ ⊇ D₊, D′₋ = D₋ being typical. Choose a, b > 0 with D′₊ ≤ aD₊ + bD₋. Take k₊ ≥ m and k₋ ≥ m + bk₊. Then the chain RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋)) → RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D′₊ − k₋D₋)) → RΓ(X̄, F̄(ak₊D₊ − (k₋ − bk₊)D₋)) → RΓ(X̄, F̄(ak₊D′₊ − (k₋ − bk₊)D₋)) becomes a chain of quasi-isomorphisms on ordinary parts.

items.name: Ordinary cohomology RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence admitting a strict dynamic compactification, F a coherent sheaf on X and T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence. The strict dynamic compactifications form a cofiltered category (Lemma 2.1.32). By Theorem 2.5.1, the complex RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F)^ord ≃ RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F)^ord, for any strict dynamic compactification (C̄, X̄, p̄₁, p̄₂, D₊, D₋), depends only on (C, X, p₁, p₂), F and T. It is denoted RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}. The support conditions are hidden in the notation.
items.note: Missing: this is the paper's central object. Its independence of choices uses Theorem 2.5.1 and the cofiltered category of strict dynamic compactifications (Lemma 2.1.32). Printed (p. 19): 'We simply denote it by RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}', with the support conditions hidden in the notation. It generalises the ordinary complexes fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), ·) of Pilloni (2020), defined there by the ordinary projector on the p-rank ≥ 1 locus, from GSp4 to any correspondence with a strict dynamic compactification.

items.name: Lemma 2.5.3: factorization of T through twists with one more pole and one more zero
items.note: Missing. The proof (pp. 19–20) starts from the map T: p̄₂*F̄(−nD₋) → p̄₁^!F̄(nD₊) of Proposition 2.3.13. Lemma 2.1.17 gives integers 0 < p < q and maps comparing p̄₂*O_X̄(qD₊) with p̄₁*O_X̄(pD₊), and likewise for D₋. Twisting, and choosing k₀ with n + (k+1)p ≤ kq for all k ≥ k₀, gives the factorisation after D₊ and D₋ are replaced by qD₊ and qD₋.

items.name: Proposition 2.5.4: ordinary cohomology is the ordinary part of the cohomology of one twisted sheaf
items.statement:
In the setting of §2.5, normalize D₊, D₋ as in Lemma 2.5.3 and let m be the integer given there. Let T act on RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋)) through the extension of Lemma 2.5.3: pullback along p̄₂, then T, then the trace along p̄₁. Then
RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F)^ord ≃ RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, F)^ord ≃ RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋))^ord
for all k₊ ≥ m and k₋ ≥ m. In particular, if A is artinian, the ordinary cohomology is represented by a bounded complex of finite A-modules.
items.note: Missing. In the proof (p. 20), the square of twisted cohomologies with the diagonal T of Lemma 2.5.3 shows that T on each corner is obtained by going once around the square. So on ordinary parts all horizontal and vertical maps are quasi-isomorphisms, as in Lemma 2.4.4(2). Remark 2.5.5 (p. 20): 'This proposition can be viewed as giving a control theorem, identifying the ordinary cohomology with the cohomology of a sheaf over X̄ with bounded zeros and poles.'

items.name: §2.6.1: the base-changed cohomological correspondence T ⊗ 1 on F ⊗_A M
items.statement:
Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence over S = Spec A admitting a strict dynamic compactification. Let F be a coherent sheaf on X which is A-flat, T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence, and M a finitely generated A-module. T ⊗ 1: p₂*(F ⊗_A M) → p₁^!(F ⊗_A M) is defined as the composite
p₂*(F ⊗_A M) = p₂*F ⊗^L_A M →^{T⊗1} p₁^!F ⊗^L_A M → p₁^!(F ⊗_A M).
The last map is adjoint to (p₁)_!(p₁^!F ⊗^L_A M) = ((p₁)_!p₁^!F) ⊗^L_A M → F ⊗_A M, which is the projection formula followed by the counit (p₁)_!p₁^! → id.
items.note: Missing. The construction needs the solid upper shriek p₁^!, the projection formula (p₁)_!(p₁^!F ⊗^L_A M) = ((p₁)_!p₁^!F) ⊗^L_A M and the counit (p₁)_!p₁^! → id (p. 21). These are targets only of the draft AnalyticStacks AS.3. Remark 2.6.3: A-flatness of F is used only to make F ⊗_A M coherent, hence bounded below.

items.name: Proposition 2.6.2: first base change formula
items.statement:
Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence over S = Spec A admitting a strict dynamic compactification. Let F be a coherent A-flat sheaf on X, T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence, and M a finitely generated (discrete) A-module. With T ⊗ 1 as in §2.6.1,
RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} ⊗^L_A M = RΓ(X, F ⊗_A M)^{C−ord}.
items.note: Missing. The proof (p. 21) first shows RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄,F) ⊗^L_A M = RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F ⊗_A M). It uses the projection formula for p̄: X̄ → S and, since j₊ is affine, Lemma 2.6.4 for (j₊)_*(j₋)_!F ⊗ p̄*M. The ordinary projectors are then applied. Remark 2.6.3: 'The assumption that M is a discrete A-module is crucial.' This is the abstract control theorem for a change of coefficients. Pilloni (2020) proves its GSp4 control theorems by hand (Theorem 11.3.1(3) there, routed to HigherHidaAndColemanTheory).

items.name: Lemma 2.6.4: tensoring a solid B-module with a discrete A-module
items.statement: Let A → B be a morphism of finitely generated Z-algebras, M ∈ D(A) a complex of discrete A-modules and N ∈ D(B■). Then N ⊗^L_{A■} M = N ⊗^L_{B■} (B ⊗^L_A M). In particular, N ⊗^L_{A■} M, which a priori is only A-solid, is B-solid.
items.note: Missing. The lemma compares solid tensor products over A■ and B■ for a map A → B of finitely generated Z-algebras. The proof (p. 21) says a B-module that is A-solid is already B-solid in this situation: it reduces to M = A^{⊕I} and uses that solid B-modules are stable under direct sums. VStackSheavesAndLisseCategories:VS2 plans solid modules and the derived solid tensor product over finitely generated Z-algebras, but not the relative structure (B,A)■ in which N ⊗^L_{A■} M a priori lives. That structure is a target only of the draft SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 (discrete Huber pairs (A,S)■).

items.name: Solid modules form a subcategory of condensed modules closed under limits and colimits
items.statement: For an analytic ring, such as B■ for a finitely generated Z-algebra B, the modules complete for its theory of measures form a full subcategory of the condensed modules over the underlying ring. This subcategory is abelian and stable under all limits, colimits and extensions. The free complete modules on extremally disconnected sets are compact projective generators. The paper uses this in the form: if N is a solid B-module, then so is N^{⊕I}.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Lemma 2.6.4, p. 21
items.note: Planned for the case the paper uses: solid modules over B■ with B a finitely generated Z-algebra. For such B, B■[S] = lim_i B[S_i] ([CSb], Theorem 8.1), which is the corrected finite-type construction VS2 asks for. VS2's node states the structure theorem for Z. The statement for a general analytic ring, [CSb] Proposition 7.5(i), is a target only of the draft SolidAnalyticRings SA.2, which is not in the atlas. Use in the paper (p. 21): 'if N is a solid B-module then N^{⊕I} is a solid B-module (the category of solid B-modules is stable under colimits inside condensed B-modules)'. External input: [CSb] (Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics), Proposition 7.5(i) (current numbering); invoked without number in the paper.

items.name: Solid quasi-coherent six functors: projection formula and proper base change
items.statement:
In the six-functor formalism for D(O_{X,■}) on schemes of finite type over Z, a separated morphism of finite type f: X → Y has a functor f_! with right adjoint f^!. Here f_! = f_* when f is proper, and for an open immersion j, j_! is extension by zero, left adjoint to j*. Two properties are used:
- projection formula: f_!(K ⊗ f*L) ≅ f_!K ⊗ L;
- proper base change: g*f_! ≅ f′_!g′* for tor-independent cartesian squares.
The paper uses the projection formula for p₁, for X̄ → S and for (j₋)_! (§2.6.1, Proposition 2.6.2, Proposition 2.3.13). It uses proper base change in the form (p₁^{(n+1)})_!(p₂^{(n+1)})* = (p₂^{(n)})*(p₁^{(n)})_! (§2.8, p. 26).
items.note: Neither library has a six-functor formalism for quasi-coherent sheaves, solid or classical. No atlas layer plans the solid one. AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:A0-extension plans only 'proper-flat coherent cohomology and base change beyond curves'. Pilloni (2020) routed Hartshorne's f^! for embeddable morphisms to that layer by a source route, which is not yet accepted. The solid formalism, including j_! for open immersions (extension by zero with completions, used throughout §2), is a target of the draft AnalyticStacks. AS.0 has 'The encoded operations ⊗, f^*, f_! and their adjoints, and the projection and base-change formulas they satisfy'. AS.3 has 'Theorem 9.7: the formalism X↦D■(X) on derived schemes almost of finite type over Z, with P proper maps, I open immersions and E separated maps'. The paper cites [CSb] Theorem 8.13 and Lecture XI for it (Lemma 2.2.2). Base change along open immersions is used in several further forms. Lemma 2.2.2(2) (p. 12) is the isomorphism p̄^⋆(j_X)_! ≅ (j_C)_!p^⋆ for a cartesian square whose horizontal maps are open immersions. The paper calls it the proper base change theorem, notes that C̄ and X are tor-independent, and cites [CSb] Theorem 8.13 and Lecture XI. The proof of Lemma 2.9.6 (p. 28) uses j^⋆(î_l)_⋆ = (î′_l)_⋆(j′)^⋆ for the open immersion j = j_{l−1} and the closed subset Ẑ_l of the locale, by means of (î_l)_⋆ = (î_l)_!. The proof of Proposition 2.9.9 (p. 29) uses two identities, p^⋆j_! = (j_C)_!p′^⋆ and j_C^⋆p^! = p′^!j^⋆. Here j : U → X is an open immersion, p : C → X is a morphism, and j_C and p′ are the base changes of j and p to C ×_X U. The second identity also uses j^⋆ = j^!. External input: [CSb] (Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics), Theorem 8.13 and Lecture XI (Coherent duality), as cited in Lemma 2.2.2 of the paper.

items.name: Lemma 2.6.6: a three-term complex of finite free modules that is exact mod m_A is split exact
items.statement: Let A be a local ring with maximal ideal m_A, and let M⁰ →^{d₀} M¹ →^{d₁} M² be a complex of finite free A-modules such that M⁰ ⊗_A A/m_A → M¹ ⊗_A A/m_A → M² ⊗_A A/m_A is exact. Then M⁰ → M¹ → M² is exact. Moreover ker(d₀) is a direct summand of M⁰, Im(d₀) is a direct summand of M¹, and Im(d₁) is a direct summand of M².
items.note: The three-term statement is in neither library. Mathlib has the two-term ingredients. IsLocalRing.split_injective_iff_lTensor_residueField_injective: a linear map from a finite module to a finite free module over a local ring is split injective iff it is injective after tensoring with the residue field. Module.free_of_lTensor_residueField_injective: freeness of a cokernel from injectivity modulo the maximal ideal. The proof (pp. 21–22) lifts a basis of ker(d₁ ⊗ A/m_A) through d₀. It completes it to a basis of M¹ ⊗ A/m_A and uses Nakayama to split M¹ = Aⁿ ⊕ Aⁿ′. It then repeats the argument for M¹/Aⁿ → M². DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra:P7 plans minimal complexes over local rings, whose construction contains this step ('lift a zero-differential complex using Lemma 15.76.5 (stably free lifts, Nakayama)'), but not this statement.

items.name: Nakayama's lemma
items.statement: Let A be a local ring with maximal ideal m and N a finitely generated A-module with N = mN. Then N = 0. Consequently, a map of finitely generated A-modules that is surjective modulo m is surjective, and a surjective map between free A-modules of the same finite rank is an isomorphism.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Lemma 2.6.6, pp. 21–22
items.note: All three assertions are in Mathlib: the lemma itself, surjectivity modulo the maximal ideal, and bijectivity of a surjection between free modules of the same finite rank. The paper uses it in the proof of Lemma 2.6.6 (pp. 21–22). External input: Nakayama's lemma (standard commutative algebra).

items.name: Lemma 2.6.7: a pseudo-coherent complex whose reduction mod m_A has amplitude [a, b] is perfect of amplitude [a, b]
items.statement: Let A be a local ring with maximal ideal m_A, and let M• be a pseudo-coherent object of the usual derived category D(A). If M• ⊗^L_A A/m_A is a perfect complex of amplitude [a, b], that is, its cohomology is concentrated in degrees [a, b], then M• is a perfect complex of amplitude [a, b]: it is quasi-isomorphic to a complex of finite free A-modules in degrees [a, b].
items.note: Planned. If K ⊗^L κ has cohomology only in degrees [a, b], the minimal complex of the P7 node has d_i = 0 outside [a, b]. So K is represented by finite free modules in degrees [a, b], which is the lemma. The paper's own proof (p. 22) truncates a bounded-above free resolution to degrees [a, b] and applies Lemma 2.6.6. Neither library has perfect complexes, pseudo-coherence or minimal complexes; the reviewed library audit of P7 records 'perfect complex' as occurring in no Lean file of either tree.

items.name: Pseudo-coherent complex
items.statement: An object of D(A) is pseudo-coherent if it is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded-above complex of finite free A-modules. For A noetherian, this is equivalent to being bounded above with finitely generated cohomology modules.
items.locator: Used in Lemma 2.6.7 and Theorem 2.6.8, p. 22 (and in §2.3)
items.note: Planned: the P7 node uses pseudo-coherence to characterise perfect complexes and as the hypothesis for minimal complexes, so the notion is part of that layer. The node does not state the Noetherian characterisation, that a bounded-above complex with finitely generated cohomology over a Noetherian ring is pseudo-coherent. The paper uses it for coherent cohomology (Lemma 2.6.7, Theorem 2.6.8, p. 22; §2.3), and the node should add it. Neither library has pseudo-coherent complexes. External input: Standard (Stacks Project, More on Algebra, section on pseudo-coherent modules).

items.name: Theorem 2.6.8: ordinary cohomology is a perfect complex over an artinian local ring
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence admitting a strict dynamic compactification, F a coherent sheaf on X, and T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence, over S = Spec A with A an artinian local ring. Assume F is A-flat. Then RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} is represented by a perfect complex of (discrete) A-modules.
items.note: Perfect complexes are planned (DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra:P7), but this theorem is not. The proof (p. 22) reduces by Lemma 2.6.7 to showing that RΓ(X,F)^{C−ord} ⊗^L_A A/m_A is bounded. By Proposition 2.6.2 with M = A/m_A this equals RΓ(X, F ⊗_A A/m_A)^{C−ord}, which is bounded by Theorem 2.5.1(2). Pseudo-coherence also comes from Theorem 2.5.1(2). This is the general form of the perfectness statements that Pilloni (2020) proves by hand for GSp4 (Proposition 8.2.1 and Theorem 11.2.1(7) there, routed to HigherHidaAndColemanTheory).

items.name: §2.6.9: equivariant cohomological correspondence and its G-coinvariants
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence over S = Spec A admitting a strict dynamic compactification, F a coherent sheaf on X and T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence. Let G be a finite abelian group acting O_X-linearly on F, and assume T commutes with the G-action, i.e. T is a map in D(O_C[G]■). Assume F is flat as an A[G]-module. Let I_G = ker(A[G] → A) be the augmentation ideal, and F/I_G := F ⊗_{A[G]} A. Then T induces a cohomological correspondence T: p₂*(F/I_G) → p₁^!(F/I_G).
items.note: No layer plans equivariant cohomological correspondences in D(O_C[G]■) or their coinvariants. The closest is the proposed IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes (Calegari–Geraghty 2018, §7.2), which is not an atlas layer. It plans perfect complexes over A[Δ] computing the coherent cohomology of a Galois cover with group Δ, with Hecke operators lifted to them, but not ordinary parts.

items.name: Theorem 2.6.10 (first part): specialization formula over A[G]
items.statement:
In the setting of §2.6.9, RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} is an object of D(A[G]), and
RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} ⊗^L_{A[G]} A = RΓ(X, F/I_G)^{C−ord}.
items.note: Missing. The printed proof (p. 22) is 'By proposition 2.6.2, we have that RΓ(X,F)^{C−ord} ⊗^L_{A[G]} A = RΓ(X, F/I_G)^{C−ord}'. Proposition 2.6.2 is stated for A-modules and an A-flat F; here it is applied with A[G] in place of A, to the A[G]-flat O_X[G]-module F. A formal proof must state this variant.

items.name: Theorem 2.6.10 (second part): perfectness over A[G]
items.statement: In the setting of §2.6.9, if A is an artinian ring, then RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} is a perfect complex of A[G]-modules.
items.note: Missing. The printed proof (p. 22): 'The final claim follows from theorem 2.6.8, as then A[G] is a product of local rings.' A[G] is finite over the artinian ring A, hence artinian and a finite product of artinian local rings. Lemma 2.6.7 is applied on each factor, with boundedness of the fibres given by the A[G]-version of Proposition 2.6.2 together with Theorem 2.5.1(2). The coherent analogue without ordinary parts is the perfect complexes over A[Δ] of the proposed IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes.

items.name: Lemma 2.6.11 (first part): the pushforward of the structure sheaf of a Galois cover is locally projective over O_X[G]
items.statement: Let r: Y → X be a finite étale cover with group G (G finite, as in §2.6.9). Then r_*O_Y is a finite locally projective sheaf of O_X[G]-modules.
items.note: Neither library has it and no atlas layer plans it. The proof (p. 22) reduces to Y = Spec C → X = Spec B. It uses C ⊗_B C ≅ C[G], c ⊗ c′ ↦ (c′g(c))_g, and the fact that C[G] is B[G]-projective because C is B-projective. It then splits C → C ⊗_B C by c ⊗ c′ ↦ c·Tr(c′c₀) with Tr(c₀) = 1. The same statement is planned, as Nakajima's lemma, in the proposed IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes (Calegari–Geraghty 2018), layer 2: 'the projectivity over k[Δ] of N ⊗_A B for a Galois étale Spec B → Spec A (Nakajima, Lemma 1)'.

items.name: Lemma 2.6.11 (second part): A[G]-flatness
items.statement: In the situation of Lemma 2.6.11, if moreover X → Spec A is flat, then r_*O_Y is A[G]-flat.
items.note: Missing, like the first part of Lemma 2.6.11: A[G]-flatness of r_*O_Y when X is flat over A, from local projectivity over O_X[G] (p. 22). It supplies the hypothesis 'F is flat as an A[G]-module' of §2.6.9 for sheaves pushed forward along Galois covers.

items.name: Trace of a finite étale surjective algebra is surjective
items.statement: If B → C is finite étale and Spec C → Spec B is surjective, then the trace Tr_{C/B}: C → B is surjective; in particular there is c₀ ∈ C with Tr(c₀) = 1.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Lemma 2.6.11, p. 22
items.note: Mathlib has surjectivity of the trace only for fields. Algebra.trace_surjective assumes [FiniteDimensional K L] [Algebra.IsSeparable K L] for fields K, L. Nothing covers finite étale algebras over a ring, and no atlas layer states it. AdicSpacesPartII:R3 plans the trace itself: 'Construct trace for finite locally free algebras and finite étale analytic maps, its base-change and composition laws, and its compatibility with algebraic trace'. The argument recorded here is standard: the image of the trace is an ideal of B, and at each prime 𝔭 of B the fibre C ⊗ k(𝔭) is a nonzero finite étale k(𝔭)-algebra with nonzero trace. The paper uses it in Lemma 2.6.11 (p. 22): 'we can choose an element c₀ in C such that Tr(c₀) = 1 since C is finite étale over B'. External input: Standard fact on finite étale algebras (the trace form is perfect, and C ⊗ k(𝔭) ≠ 0 for every prime 𝔭 of B).

items.name: §2.6.12: base change of a correspondence along a finite S′ → S
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence over S = Spec A admitting a strict dynamic compactification, and S′ = Spec A′ → S a finite morphism. Put X′ = X ×_S S′, C′ = C ×_S S′, with the base-changed projections p′ᵢ. Then (C′, X′, p′₁, p′₂) admits a strict dynamic compactification: the base change along S′ → S of one of (C, X, p₁, p₂). Let F be a coherent A-flat sheaf on X, T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence, and F′ the pullback of F to X′. Assuming X and S′ tor-independent over S, the paper deduces by base change a cohomological correspondence T′: (p′₂)*F′ → (p′₁)^!F′, citing [CSb], Proposition 11.4.
items.note: Missing. Strict dynamic compactifications base change along S′ → S (p. 22). The base-changed correspondence T′ needs flat or tor-independent base change for the solid upper shriek, which the paper takes from [CSb] Proposition 11.4 (p. 23). That is a target only of the draft AnalyticStacks AS.3.

items.name: Clausen–Scholze, Proposition 11.4: f^! as a twist of f*, and flat base change for f^!
items.statement: Let f: R → B be a ring map that is the base change of a finitely generated map of finite Tor-dimension between noetherian rings. Then the natural map f^!R ⊗^L_{B■} f*(−) → f^!(−) of functors D(R■) → D(B■) is an equivalence. Moreover, if g: R → R′ is flat, f′: R′ → B′ = B ⊗_R R′ is the base change of f and g′: B → B′, there is a natural equivalence g′*f^! ≃ f′^!g*. The comparison map is adjoint to f^! → f^!g_*g* ≃ g′_*f′^!g*, which uses the equivalence f^!g_* ≃ g′_*f′^! adjoint to proper base change.
items.locator: Cited on p. 23 (§2.6.12) and p. 25 (construction of T_n)
items.note: Neither library has it. The statement matches Proposition 11.4 of the current Clausen–Scholze notes: 'the natural map f^!R ⊗^L_{A■} f^* → f^! of functors D(R■) → D(A■) is an equivalence', with the flat base change g′^*f^! ≃ f′^!g^*. No atlas layer plans it. The draft AnalyticStacks AS.3 has it as part of 'Theorem 9.17 ... maps of finite Tor-dimension are suave'. Pilloni (2020)'s Hartshorne-style base change of f^!O_Y (Proposition 4.2.5.1 there) was routed by source to AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:A0-extension. The two constructions must be compared wherever both are used. The paper uses it on p. 23 (§2.6.12) and p. 25 (construction of T_n). External input: [CSb] (Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics), Proposition 11.4 in Lecture XI, as numbered in the current (May 2026) version.

items.name: Proposition 2.6.13: second base change formula (finite base change)
items.statement:
Under the assumptions of §2.6.12, with the cohomological correspondence T′ on F′ over X′,
RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} ⊗^L_A A′ = RΓ(X′, F′)^{C′−ord}.
items.note: Missing. The proof (p. 23) argues as in Proposition 2.6.2 that RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄,F) ⊗^L_A A′ = RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, F ⊗^L_A A′). By tor-independence O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, so F ⊗^L_A A′ = F′. The ordinary projectors are then applied.

items.name: Duality functors D_S and D_X (§2.7)
items.statement: Let p: X → S be a separated morphism of finite type between schemes of finite type over Z. Put D_S := RHom(−, O_S) on D(O_{S,■}) and D_X := RHom(−, p^!O_S) on D(O_{X,■}), where RHom is the internal Hom.
items.note: Missing. Internal RHom in D(O_{X,■}) and the solid p^! are in neither library. They are targets only of the draft AnalyticStacks AS.3, whose dualizing-complex statement reads 'f is cohomologically smooth in D■ with dualizing complex Ω^d_{X/Y}[d]'. Grothendieck–Serre duality for higher-dimensional schemes is not an atlas target. It reaches A0-extension only through source routes from other papers, and Serre duality is planned only for curves (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3).

items.name: Theorem 2.7.1: p_* D_X = D_S p_!
items.statement: Let p: X → S be a separated morphism of finite type between schemes of finite type over Z, and F ∈ D(O_{X,■}). Then p_* D_X(F) = D_S(p_! F).
items.note: Missing. The paper calls it 'a restatement of the adjunction property between p_! and p^!' (p. 23), so it is a formal consequence of the solid six functors (the projection formula and p_! ⊣ p^!). Those are targets only of the draft AnalyticStacks (AS.0 and AS.3). Neither library has coherent Grothendieck duality. Pilloni (2020)'s Hartshorne duality for projectively embeddable morphisms was routed by source to AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:A0-extension. The solid and classical dualities must be compared where both are used. External input: [CSb] (Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics), Lecture XI: Verdier duality f_*RHom(A, f^!B) ≅ RHom(f_!A, B) in the six-functor formalism of solid quasi-coherent sheaves.

items.name: Stupid truncation σ_{≤m}
items.statement: For a complex K, the stupid truncation σ_{≤m}K is the complex with the terms K^i for i ≤ m and 0 in degrees > m. It is a quotient complex of K, and K = lim_m σ_{≤m}K. Unlike the canonical truncation, it is not invariant under quasi-isomorphism.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Proposition 2.7.2, p. 23
items.note: The definition is in Mathlib. The quotient map K → σ_{≤m}K is not: it appears as a TODO next to the definition ('define the projection 𝟭 _ ⟶ e.stupidTruncFunctor C when [e.IsTruncLE]'). The identity K = lim_m σ_{≤m}K is also absent. Both are short additions. The paper uses the truncations (p̄^!O_S)^{σ≤m} in the proof of Proposition 2.7.2 (p. 23), citing Stacks Tag 0118. External input: Stacks Project, Tag 0118 (as cited in the paper).

items.name: f^! for smooth morphisms and for morphisms of finite Tor-dimension
items.statement: (Clausen–Scholze) For f: X → Spec R smooth, separated and of finite type of relative dimension d, f^!R ≅ ω_{X/R}[d] with ω_{X/R} = det Ω¹_{X/R}, an invertible object. For f of finite Tor-dimension, f^!M = f*M ⊗ f^!R. The paper uses three consequences: for p: X → S smooth, p^!O_S is a shifted line bundle; for C and X smooth over S, p₁^!O_X is invertible; and p_i^!K = p_i^!O_X ⊗ p_i*K.
items.locator: Used in the proofs of Propositions 2.7.2 and 2.7.3, pp. 23–24
items.note: Neither library has it, and no atlas layer plans the solid f^!. The draft AnalyticStacks AS.3 has exactly this target: 'Theorem 9.17: for a smooth map f:X→Y of derived schemes, f is cohomologically smooth in D■ with dualizing complex Ω^d_{X/Y}[d]; maps of finite Tor-dimension are suave; for local complete intersections f^!1 is invertible and isomorphic to det(L_{X/Y})'. The Clausen–Scholze statements (Theorems 11.1 and 11.6: f^!R ≅ det_A(Ω¹_{A/R})[d] for smooth f of dimension d; Proposition 11.4) were checked against the current notes. Pilloni (2020)'s classical versions (h^!O_S = ω_{X/S}[n] for lci h, and f^!O_Y = ω_{X/S} ⊗ f^*ω_{Y/S}^{−1}) were routed to AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:A0-extension. External input: [CSb] (Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics), Theorems 11.1 and 11.6, Theorem 8.13(iv), Proposition 11.4.

items.name: Proposition 2.7.2: duality exchanges the two partial supports
items.statement:
Let S = Spec A and p: X → S smooth. Let X ↪ X̄ be an open immersion with X̄ proper over S and X̄ ∖ X = D₁ ∪ D₂, where D₁ and D₂ are Cartier divisors. Let F be a locally free sheaf of finite rank on X that extends to a locally free sheaf F̄ on X̄. Then
RHom_A(RΓ_{D₁,−, D₂,+}(X̄, F), A) = RΓ_{D₁,+, D₂,−}(X̄, D_X(F)).
The subscripts indicate roles. RΓ_{D₁,−,D₂,+}(X̄, F) is RΓ_{D₋,D₊} with D₋ = D₁ and D₊ = D₂, i.e. RΓ(X̄, (j₁)_!(j₂)_*F) for X ↪^{j₂} X̄∖D₁ ↪^{j₁} X̄. RΓ_{D₁,+,D₂,−}(X̄, D_X(F)) = RΓ(X̄, (j₁)_*(j₂)_!D_X(F)).
items.note: Missing. The proof (p. 23) uses Theorem 2.7.1 to reduce to D_X̄(j_*F) = j_!D_X(F) for j: X → X̄ with complement V(I), I invertible. Writing j_*F = colim I^{−n}F gives D_X̄(j_*F) = lim_n Iⁿ RHom(F, p̄^!O_S). Replacing p̄^!O_S by its stupid truncations σ_{≤m} makes the terms pseudo-coherent, so Proposition 2.3.2 applies; since p is smooth, σ_{≤m}(p^!O_S) = p^!O_S for m large. It depends on the solid duality of Theorem 2.7.1 and on the partial-support formalism.

items.name: Proposition 2.7.3: the transpose of a cohomological correspondence
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence with C and X smooth over S, F a locally free sheaf of finite rank on X, and T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence. Let D_C = RHom(−, q^!O_S) with q: C → S. Then D_C(p₂*F) = p₂^!D_X(F) and D_C(p₁^!F) = p₁*D_X(F). Hence applying D_C to T gives a cohomological correspondence T^t: p₁*D_X(F) → p₂^!D_X(F), the transpose, for the transposed correspondence (C, X, p₂, p₁).
items.note: Missing. The proof (pp. 23–24) computes D_C(p₂*F) = p₂^!p^!O_S ⊗ (p₂*F)^∨ = p₂^!D_X(F). Because C and X are smooth over S, p₁^!O_X is invertible, which gives D_C(p₁^!F) = p₁*D_X(F). Coherent cohomological correspondences p₂*F → p₁^!G (Pilloni 2020, Remark 4.3.2) and the duality pairings behind Hecke operators (Calegari–Geraghty 2018, §7.2) were both routed to the proposed IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes, which is not an atlas layer. The transpose is a general operation on such correspondences, with no compactification hypothesis.

items.name: Transposed correspondence C^t and its dynamic compactification
items.statement: For a correspondence (C, X, p₁, p₂), the transpose is (C, X, p₂, p₁). If C = (C̄, X̄, p̄₁, p̄₂, D₊, D₋) is a (strict) dynamic compactification of (C, X, p₁, p₂), then C^t := (C̄, X̄, p̄₂, p̄₁, D₊^t, D₋^t), with D₊^t = D₋ and D₋^t = D₊, is a (strict) dynamic compactification of the transpose. With the cohomological correspondence T^t on D_X(F) (Proposition 2.7.3), RΓ(X, D_X(F))^{C^t−ord} denotes the corresponding ordinary cohomology.
items.note: Missing, together with dynamic compactifications (§2.1). Exchanging p₁ and p₂ swaps the roles of D₊ and D₋, so C^t = (C̄, X̄, p̄₂, p̄₁, D₋, D₊) is a strict dynamic compactification of the transpose whenever C is one (p. 24, proof of Theorem 2.7.4).

items.name: Theorem 2.7.4: duality between the ordinary cohomology of C and of C^t
items.statement:
Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence with C and X smooth over S = Spec A, admitting a strict dynamic compactification, with A artinian. Let F be a locally free sheaf of finite rank on X, T: p₂*F → p₁^!F a cohomological correspondence, and C^t, T^t the transposes. Then there is a perfect pairing
RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} × RΓ(X, D_X(F))^{C^t−ord} → A.
That is, RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} = RHom_A(RΓ(X, D_X(F))^{C^t−ord}, A) and RΓ(X, D_X(F))^{C^t−ord} = RHom_A(RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}, A).
items.note: Missing. The proof (p. 24) chooses a compactification on which F extends to a locally free sheaf and D± are Cartier (Lemmas 2.1.6, 2.1.12, 2.1.30). Proposition 2.7.2 then gives RHom(RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄,F), A) = RΓ_{D₊^t,D₋^t}(X̄, D_X(F)), equivariantly for T and T^t by Proposition 2.7.3. Lemma 2.4.4 splits both sides into ordinary and non-ordinary parts, and the non-ordinary parts are A[[T]]-modules. The ordinary parts match because 'A[T,T⁻¹]■ ⊗_{A[T]} A[[T]] = 0'.

items.name: Iterated correspondences C^{(n)} (§2.8)
items.statement:
Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence. Put C^{(0)} = X, C^{(1)} = C and p_i^{(1)} = p_i. Inductively, for n ≥ 2, let
C^{(n)} := C^{(n−1)} ×_{p₁^{(n−1)}, C^{(n−2)}, p₂^{(n−1)}} C^{(n−1)},
with p₂^{(n)}: C^{(n)} → C^{(n−1)} the projection to the first factor and p₁^{(n)} the projection to the second factor. Then (C^{(n)}, C^{(n−1)}, p₁^{(n)}, p₂^{(n)}) is a correspondence on C^{(n−1)}.
items.note: Mathlib has fibre products of schemes (its HasPullbacks instance for Scheme), so each C^{(n)} can be formed. The notion of a correspondence (C, X, p₁, p₂) with p₁ × p₂ proper, from §2.1, is in neither library, and no atlas layer plans iterated correspondences. C^{(n)} is the correspondence whose action is Tⁿ.

items.name: Lemma 2.8.1: iterated correspondences inherit (strict, compact) dynamic compactifications
items.note: Missing. The proof (pp. 24–25) is by induction. From (p̄₂^{(n)})*D₊^{(n−1)} ⊆ (p̄₁^{(n)})*D₊^{(n−1)} and the commutation (p̄₁^{(n+1)})*(p̄₂^{(n)})* = (p̄₂^{(n+1)})*(p̄₁^{(n)})* on the fibre square, it gets (p̄₂^{(n+1)})*D₊^{(n)} ⊆ (p̄₁^{(n+1)})*D₊^{(n)}, and similarly for D₋. The strict and compact variants 'are checked easily' (p. 25).

items.name: Iterated cohomological correspondences T_n (§2.8)
items.statement: Let T: p₂*O_X → p₁^!O_X be a cohomological correspondence and assume p₁ and p₂ are flat. Put T₁ = T. Given T_n: (p₂^{(n)})*O_{C^{(n−1)}} → (p₁^{(n)})^!O_{C^{(n−1)}}, define T_{n+1} := (p₂^{(n+1)})*T_n. Its source is (p₂^{(n+1)})*(p₂^{(n)})*O_{C^{(n−1)}} = (p₂^{(n+1)})*O_{C^{(n)}}. Its target is (p₂^{(n+1)})*(p₁^{(n)})^!O_{C^{(n−1)}} = (p₁^{(n+1)})^!O_{C^{(n)}}, by flat base change for the cartesian square defining C^{(n+1)} ([CSb], Proposition 11.4). Then T_n is a cohomological correspondence on O_{C^{(n−1)}} for (C^{(n)}, C^{(n−1)}, p₁^{(n)}, p₂^{(n)}). If (C, X, p₁, p₂) admits a strict dynamic compactification, then RΓ_n := RΓ(C^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}})^{C^{(n+1)}−ord}, the ordinary part for T_{n+1}, is defined (Lemma 2.8.1, Theorem 2.5.1).
items.note: Missing. T_{n+1} = (p₂^{(n+1)})*T_n. The identification (p₂^{(n+1)})*(p₁^{(n)})^!O = (p₁^{(n+1)})^!O is flat base change for the solid upper shriek ([CSb] Proposition 11.4, p. 25), a target only of the draft AnalyticStacks AS.3. The ordinary cohomology RΓ_n is then defined by Lemma 2.8.1 and Theorem 2.5.1.

items.name: Commutativity of the square (2.8.A): trace and pullback commute along the iterated correspondences
items.statement:
Assume p₁ and p₂ are flat and that (C, X, p₁, p₂) admits a strict dynamic compactification. Let RΓ′_n := RΓ_{D₊^{(n)}, D₋^{(n)}}(C̄^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}}), so that RΓ′_0 = RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, O_X). Let (p₂^{(n)})*: RΓ′_{n−1} → RΓ′_n be the pullback (with the changes of support of Lemmas 2.2.6 and 2.2.7). Let (p₁^{(n)})_!: RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n−1} be T_n followed by the trace along p̄₁^{(n)}. Thus (p₁^{(n)})_!∘(p₂^{(n)})* is the endomorphism of RΓ′_{n−1} induced by T_n. Then for n ≥ 1,
(p₁^{(n+1)})_! ∘ (p₂^{(n+1)})* = (p₂^{(n)})* ∘ (p₁^{(n)})_!
as endomorphisms of RΓ′_n.
items.note: Missing. The proof (pp. 26–27) reduces the square to proper base change (p₁^{(n+1)})_!(p₂^{(n+1)})* = (p₂^{(n)})*(p₁^{(n)})_!. It is compatible with the supports: since p̃₁^{(n+1)} and p̄₁^{(n+1)} are proper, (p̄₁^{(n+1)})_!(j₊^{(n+1)})_* = (j₊^{(n)})_*(p̃₁^{(n+1)})_! and (p̃₁^{(n+1)})_!(j₋^{(n+1)})_! = (j₋^{(n)})_!(p₁^{(n+1)})_!. The other ingredients are Lemma 2.2.2 and the construction of T_{n+1} from T_n. The six-functor inputs are targets only of the draft AnalyticStacks AS.3.

items.name: Proposition 2.8.2: ordinary cohomology can be computed on the iterated correspondences
items.statement:
Assume p₁ and p₂ are flat, T: p₂*O_X → p₁^!O_X is a cohomological correspondence, and (C, X, p₁, p₂) admits a strict dynamic compactification (implicit in the paper). Let RΓ_n = RΓ(C^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}})^{C^{(n+1)}−ord}. The maps (p₂^{(n+1)})*: RΓ_n → RΓ_{n+1} and (p₁^{(n+1)})_!: RΓ_{n+1} → RΓ_n form a commutative diagram: the zigzag RΓ₀ → RΓ₁ → RΓ₀ → RΓ₁ → ⋯, with RΓ₁ → RΓ₂ → RΓ₁ above each RΓ₁ → RΓ₀ → RΓ₁, and so on. All maps in it are quasi-isomorphisms. Hence, for every n ≥ 0,
RΓ(C^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}})^{C^{(n+1)}−ord} ≃ RΓ(X, O_X)^{C−ord}.
items.note: Missing. The zigzag of pullbacks and traces between RΓ′_n commutes by the square (2.8.A). The composite trace∘pullback is the endomorphism T_n, which is invertible on ordinary parts, so every map in the diagram becomes a quasi-isomorphism on ordinary parts (pp. 25–27). As the item records, the hypothesis that (C, X, p₁, p₂) has a strict dynamic compactification is implicit in the paper. Compare the correspondence C_m of U^m used in Pilloni (2020), proof of Theorem 11.3.1, to compare ordinary cohomology at two levels for GSp4; that item was routed to HigherHidaAndColemanTheory.

items.name: Artinian rings are finite products of artinian local rings
items.statement: An artinian ring is a finite product of artinian local rings, and a finite algebra over an artinian ring is artinian. The maximal ideal of an artinian local ring is nilpotent.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3, p. 18, and of Theorem 2.6.10, p. 22
items.note: All three assertions follow from Mathlib declarations; the product decomposition needs a two-line assembly. The paper uses them in Lemma 2.4.3 (p. 18), Lemma 2.4.4(3) (p. 19) and Theorem 2.6.10 (p. 22: 'A[G] is a product of local rings'). External input: Standard commutative algebra (e.g. Atiyah–Macdonald, Chapter 8).

items.name: The completed algebra R̂^I, the locale-closed subset Ẑ and the functor î_⋆î^⋆
items.statement:
Standing assumption of §2.2: all schemes are of finite type over Z. D(R_■) is the derived category of solid R-modules, and D(𝒪_{X,■}) is the derived category of solid quasi-coherent 𝒪_X-modules.

Affine case. Let X = Spec R, let I ⊆ R be an ideal, let U = X ∖ V(I) with open immersion j : U ↪ X, and let Z be the closed complement of U. As a closed subscheme of X, Z = Spec R/J for any choice of ideal J with √J = √I. Z can also be viewed as a closed subset of the locale of D(R_■). Its algebra of functions is then the idempotent solid R-algebra R̂^I = lim_n R/I^n (Lemma 2.9.2). Viewed this way Z is written Ẑ, and î : Ẑ → X is the corresponding 'closed immersion'. Concretely, there is a functor î_⋆î^⋆ : D(R_■) → D(R_■), M ↦ M ⊗_R R̂^I (solid derived tensor product), and its essential image is written D((R̂^I, R)_■).

Global case. Let i : Z ↪ X be a closed subscheme of a scheme X, defined by the ideal sheaf 𝓘, with open complement j : U → X. Then î : Ẑ ↪ X is the corresponding closed subset of the locale of X. For F ∈ D(𝒪_{X,■}), by definition î_⋆î^⋆F = F ⊗_{𝒪_X} lim_n(𝒪_X/𝓘^n).
items.note:
The closed subset of the locale and its algebra are planned in the new roadmap SolidAnalyticRings. That roadmap follows J. E. Rodríguez Camargo, Notes on solid geometry (arXiv:2603.03012v1).
- SA.2 plans the smashing spectrum of §5.1 of those notes: closed subsets correspond to idempotent algebras (Proposition 5.1.2), and closed immersions are those of Definition 5.1.3 and Proposition 5.1.4. Remark 5.1.5 in that section writes the pullback to the closed subset as ι^*M = A ⊗ M (p. 47). With A = R̂^I this is the paper's î_⋆î^⋆M = M ⊗_R R̂^I.
- SA.3 plans Proposition 5.3.12. Part (2) states that for R of finite type over Z and I finitely generated, R̂^I is an idempotent R_□-algebra (p. 56).
- SA.3 also plans Proposition 5.4.15. Its proof identifies the closed complement of Spec R[1/f] with the idempotent algebra R[[X]]/(X − f) (p. 63), so Ẑ is the closed complement of U.
The global category D(𝒪_{X,■}) is AnalyticStacks AS.3's solid formalism on schemes, and lim_n 𝒪_X/𝓘^n is glued from the affine algebras R̂^I. Both roadmaps work with light condensed sets, while the paper uses the κ-condensed setting of Clausen–Scholze. The objects §2.9 needs are finite-type rings, their I-adic completions, finite free modules and countable products, and the light theory treats all of them.

items.name: Lemma 2.9.2: R̂^I is an idempotent algebra in D(R_■)
items.statement:
Let R be a ring of finite type over Z (standing assumption; the proof uses that R is noetherian) and I ⊆ R an ideal. Then the solid R-algebra R̂^I = lim_n R/I^n is an idempotent algebra in D(R_■), i.e. R̂^I ⊗_R R̂^I ≅ R̂^I (derived solid tensor product).

The proof also gives the following.
(a) If I = (f), there is an exact sequence 0 → R[[X]] --(X−f)--> R[[X]] → R̂^I → 0, and R̂^I ⊗_R R[[X]] = R̂^I[[X]].
(b) If I = (f₁, …, f_r), then R̂^{(f₁,…,f_r)} ≅ ⊗_{i=1}^r R̂^{(f_i)}. This is a compact object of D(R_■), represented by a bounded complex whose terms are of the form R^ℕ. Moreover R̂^{(f₁,…,f_{r−1})} ⊗_R R̂^{(f_r)} = [R̂^{(f₁,…,f_{r−1})}[[X]] --(X−f_r)--> R̂^{(f₁,…,f_{r−1})}[[X]]] = R̂^{(f₁,…,f_r)}.
items.note:
Planned in SolidAnalyticRings SA.3, which lists Proposition 5.3.12 of Rodríguez Camargo's Notes on solid geometry (p. 56). For R of finite type over Z and finitely generated ideals I and J, it states:
- (1) R̂^I is pseudo-compact, and R̂^I ⊗_{R_□} ∏_N R = ∏_N R̂^I;
- (2) R̂^I ⊗_{R_□} R̂^J = R̂^{I+J}, 'In particular, R̂^I is an idempotent R_□-algebra'.
Part (b) of the lemma is (2) iterated. The presentation in (a) is the one in the proof of Proposition 5.4.15, which SA.3 also lists: the closed complement of Spec R[1/f] is 'the idempotent R_□-algebra R[[f_i]] … also given by the derived quotient R[[X]]/^L(X − f_i)' (p. 63). The model case over Z[q] is among SA.1's computations, Example 3.5.1: Z[[q]] ⊗^L_{Z[q]} Z[[q]] = Z[[q]]. Over a noetherian R, X − f is injective on R[[X]] (Krull's intersection theorem; checked by direct computation). So the derived quotient is R̂^{(f)} = lim_n R/f^n, as the paper states.

items.name: Solid tensor products of power series rings and of products
items.statement: Let R be a ring of finite type over Z. In D(R_■), R[[X]] ⊗_R R[[X′]] ≅ R[[X, X′]] (solid tensor product). More generally, for any sets I and J, ∏_I R ⊗_R ∏_J R ≅ ∏_{I×J} R. The power series case is I = J = ℕ, with R[[X]] = ∏_ℕ R. As used in the text, this gives: P ⊗_R R[[X]] = P[[X]] for P a bounded complex of objects R^ℕ, and R^J ⊗_R P = P^J for any set J and any such P, in particular for P = R̂^I.
items.locator: proof of Lemma 2.9.2, p. 27; proof of Lemma 2.9.3, p. 28
items.note:
Planned.
- Over Z, SolidAnalyticRings SA.1 lists among its computations '∏_N Z ⊗^□ ∏_N Z = ∏_{N×N} Z, Z[[T]] ⊗^□ Z[[S]] = Z[[T,S]]'.
- Over a finite-type R, SA.3 plans Theorem 5.3.2 of Rodríguez Camargo's notes: R_□[S] = lim_n R[S_n], and ∏_N R is flat. It also plans Proposition 5.3.12(1): R̂^I ⊗ ∏_N R = ∏_N R̂^I.
Since R_□[N ∪ {∞}] ≅ ∏_N R ≅ R[[X]], and the solid tensor product of free objects is free on the product of the profinite sets, these give R[[X]] ⊗_R R[[X′]] = R[[X, X′]]. They also give P ⊗_R R[[X]] = P[[X]] for a bounded complex P of copies of ∏_N R.
The layers are light-condensed and treat countable products. The paper states the fact for arbitrary index sets. This is the κ-condensed Proposition 6.3 of Scholze's Lectures on Condensed Mathematics: ∏_I Z ⊗^L_□ ∏_J Z = ∏_{I×J} Z. The proof of Lemma 2.9.3 uses R^J for an arbitrary set J, but for a coherent sheaf, the case the paper applies, finite free modules suffice. Mathlib has only the predicate CondensedMod.IsSolid and the solidification of free condensed modules on profinite sets. It has no solid tensor product. External input: Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics ([CSb]): the solid theory over finite type Z-algebras, in which products ∏_I R are compact projective and ∏_I R ⊗ ∏_J R = ∏_{I×J} R. The paper uses these facts without a precise reference.

items.name: The two localization triangles for U ↪ X ↩ Ẑ
items.statement:
Affine case. In the setting of §2.9.1 (X = Spec R, U = X ∖ V(I), j : U ↪ X, î : Ẑ → X), for every M ∈ D(R_■) there are exact triangles
j_!j^⋆M → M → î_⋆î^⋆M →(+1),
î_⋆î^!M → M → j_⋆j^⋆M →(+1).
Here j_⋆, j_!, j^⋆ are the functors of the six-functor formalism for the open immersion U ↪ X.

Global case. Let X be a scheme (of finite type over Z), i : Z ↪ X a closed subscheme with open complement j : U → X, and î : Ẑ ↪ X the corresponding closed subset of the locale. Then every F ∈ D(𝒪_{X,■}) sits in exact triangles
j_!j^⋆F → F → î_⋆î^⋆F →(+1),
î_⋆î^!F → F → j_⋆j^⋆F →(+1).
items.note:
Planned.
- SolidAnalyticRings SA.2 plans the open and closed immersions of §5.1 of Rodríguez Camargo's notes. Remark 5.1.5 there treats an idempotent algebra A, with closed immersion ι and open complement j (p. 47). It gives ι^*M = A ⊗ M, ι_*ι^!M = Hom(A, M), j_!j^*M = fib(1 → A) ⊗ M and j_*j^*M = Hom(fib(1 → A), M). Tensoring M with the fibre sequence fib(1 → A) → 1 → A gives the first triangle, and applying Hom(−, M) to it gives the second.
- SA.3 plans Proposition 5.4.15 and Theorem 5.4.16, which identify the open complement of R̂^{(f)} with Spec R[1/f]. For I = (f₁, …, f_r) the closed subset is the intersection of the V(f_i). Its algebra is ⊗_i R̂^{(f_i)} = R̂^I, by Propositions 5.1.2(1) and 5.3.12(2). So j is the open immersion of schemes U ↪ X.
- AnalyticStacks AS.2 plans the same excision triangle for analytic stacks.
- AS.3 plans the solid formalism on schemes of finite type over Z (Scholze's Theorem 9.7, with open immersions in the class I). With it, the global case follows by Zariski descent. External input: Clausen–Scholze, Condensed mathematics and complex geometry ([CSa]), lecture V (the open–closed decomposition attached to an idempotent algebra), which the paper applies to this setting. The six-functor formalism for solid quasi-coherent sheaves is from [CSb], lecture XI.

items.name: Lemma 2.9.3: î_⋆î^⋆ of a pseudo-coherent complex is the limit of its reductions
items.statement:
Let X be a scheme (of finite type over Z) and Z ⊆ X a closed subscheme with ideal sheaf 𝓘, and let î : Ẑ ↪ X be the corresponding closed subset of the locale. If F ∈ D(𝒪_{X,■}) is pseudo-coherent, then
î_⋆î^⋆F = lim_n (F ⊗_{𝒪_X} 𝒪_X/𝓘^n)
and
RΓ(X, î_⋆î^⋆F) = lim_n RΓ(X, F ⊗_{𝒪_X} 𝒪_X/𝓘^n).
items.note:
Missing as stated, but its affine core is close to planned material.
- SolidAnalyticRings SA.3 plans Proposition 5.3.12 of Rodríguez Camargo's notes. Part (1) is the case M = ∏_N R: R̂^I ⊗_{R_□} ∏_N R = ∏_N R̂^I (p. 56).
- Lemma 5.3.10(3) in the same section gives lim_n P_n ⊗ lim_n Q_n = lim_n (P_n ⊗ Q_n) for sequential diagrams of connective pseudo-compact modules (p. 55). Applied, after a shift, to a constant diagram P_n = M and to Q_n = R/I^n, it gives the affine statement.
SA.3 names neither Lemma 5.3.10 nor pseudo-coherent objects. No layer states the sheaf version on a scheme X. None states the identity RΓ(X, î_⋆î^⋆F) = lim_n RΓ(X, F ⊗ 𝒪_X/𝓘^n) either, although it follows from the first identity because RΓ commutes with limits.

items.name: Remark 2.9.4: the localization triangle as limits (compatibility with Proposition 2.3.2)
items.statement: Let X be a scheme (of finite type over Z), Z = V(𝓘) ⊆ X a closed subscheme with open complement j : U ↪ X, and F ∈ D(O_{X,■}) pseudo-coherent. By Lemma 2.9.3, the triangle j_!j^⋆F → F → î_⋆î^⋆F →(+1) reads lim_n 𝓘^n ⊗ F → F → lim_n F ⊗ O_X/𝓘^n →(+1). This is compatible with Proposition 2.3.2: when Z is locally principal, with O_X(−Z) → O_X having image 𝓘, that proposition gives j_!j^⋆F = lim_n F(−nZ), where F(−nZ) = F ⊗ O_X(−Z)^{⊗n}.
items.note: Missing. It follows from Lemma 2.9.3 and the first localization triangle, which is planned. Pass to the limit over n in the triangles 𝓘^n ⊗ F → F → F ⊗ 𝒪_X/𝓘^n; this gives j_!j^⋆F = lim_n 𝓘^n ⊗ F. No layer states it. The compatibility it asserts is with Proposition 2.3.2 of §2.3, which says j_!F = lim_n F(−nD) when the complement D is locally principal.

items.name: §2.9.5: cohomologies attached to a filtration by closed subschemes
items.note:
Missing as a named construction, although every functor in it is planned.
- (j_l)_!, (j_l)^⋆ and RΓ come from the solid formalism on schemes of finite type over Z (AnalyticStacks AS.3, Scholze's Theorem 9.7).
- (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆ = − ⊗ lim_n 𝒪_X/𝓘_l^n comes from the idempotent completion algebras (SolidAnalyticRings SA.2 and SA.3).
- The triangles RΓ_c(U_l, F) → RΓ(X, F) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, F) are the planned localization triangles.
No layer defines the cohomology of a formal completion along a closed stratum. None defines the compactly supported cohomology of the difference Ẑ_l ∖ Ẑ_{l−1} of two such completions either.

items.name: Lemma 2.9.6 (first assertion): commuting j_! j^⋆ past î_⋆ î^⋆
items.note: Missing, though it is immediate from planned formulas. Rodríguez Camargo's Remark 5.1.5, in SolidAnalyticRings SA.2, gives (j_{l−1})_!(j_{l−1})^⋆M = fib(1 → A_{l−1}) ⊗ M and (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆M = A_l ⊗ M, where A_l is the idempotent algebra of Ẑ_l. So both composites are M ↦ fib(1 → A_{l−1}) ⊗ A_l ⊗ M. The paper argues instead by proper base change for the closed immersion of the locale: (j_{l−1})^⋆(î_l)_⋆ = (î′_l)_⋆(j′_{l−1})^⋆. No layer states the commutation.

items.name: Lemma 2.9.6 (triangles): the two exact triangles for the strata
items.statement:
In the setting of §2.9.5, for 0 ≤ l ≤ d and F ∈ D(𝒪_{X,■}) there are exact triangles
RΓ_c(Ẑ_l ∖ Ẑ_{l−1}, F) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, F) → RΓ(Ẑ_{l−1}, F) →(+1),
RΓ_c(U_l, F) → RΓ_c(U_{l−1}, F) → RΓ_c(Ẑ_l ∖ Ẑ_{l−1}, F) →(+1).
items.note:
Missing. Both triangles come from the planned localization triangles, applied to (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆F and to (j_{l−1})_!(j_{l−1})^⋆F. They also use two absorption identities that hold because Z_{l−1} ⊆ Z_l:
- (î_{l−1})_⋆(î_{l−1})^⋆(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆ = (î_{l−1})_⋆(î_{l−1})^⋆. This is Proposition 5.1.2(2) of Rodríguez Camargo's notes, 'Z ⊂ Z′ if and only if A ⊗ A′ = A', planned in SolidAnalyticRings SA.2.
- (j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆(j_{l−1})_!(j_{l−1})^⋆ = (j_l)_!(j_l)^⋆, because j_{l−1}^⋆(j_{l−1})_! = Id.
No layer states the triangles for strata.

items.name: Theorem 2.9.7: the Cousin spectral sequence of a filtration
items.statement:
Standing assumptions of §2: schemes are of finite type over Z, over the base S = Spec A. Let X be a scheme with a filtration Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z₀ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ Z_d = X by closed subschemes (notation of §2.9.5), and let F ∈ D^−(O_{X,■}). Then there is a spectral sequence
E₁^{p,q} = H_c^{p+q}(Ẑ_p ∖ Ẑ_{p−1}, F) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X, F), for 0 ≤ p ≤ d.
It is the spectral sequence of a filtered complex, constructed as follows. Represent each RΓ_c(U_i, F), −1 ≤ i ≤ d − 1, which lies in D^−(A_■), by a bounded above complex A_i^• of projective solid A-modules; this uses that X is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Take maps A_{d−1}^• → A_{d−2}^• → ⋯ → A_{−1}^• representing RΓ_c(U_{d−1}, F) → ⋯ → RΓ_c(U_{−1}, F) = RΓ(X, F). Replace the A_i^• by homotopy equivalent bounded above complexes so that each A_i^• → A_{i−1}^• is a termwise split injection. Then A_{−1}^• is filtered by the subcomplexes F^pA_{−1}^• = A_{p−1}^•, 0 ≤ p ≤ d + 1 (with A_d^• = 0). By Lemma 2.9.6 the p-th graded piece A_{p−1}^•/A_p^• represents RΓ_c(Ẑ_p ∖ Ẑ_{p−1}, F).
items.note:
Missing. Some of its inputs are planned or partly available:
- The spectral sequence of a finite filtered complex falls under FoundationsAndLibraryIntegration LI.3 ('spectral sequences').
- Mathlib constructs spectral sequences of spectral objects, but not their convergence.
- Projective representatives in D^−(A_■) come from the compact projective generators of solid modules over a finite-type ring (SolidAnalyticRings SA.3, Theorem 5.3.2).
Other inputs are not planned:
- The replacement of the chain RΓ_c(U_{d−1}, F) → ⋯ → RΓ(X, F) by termwise split injections (Stacks Project, Lemma 13.9.15).
- The identification of the graded pieces with RΓ_c(Ẑ_p ∖ Ẑ_{p−1}, F) (Lemma 2.9.6).
No layer plans a Cousin or coniveau spectral sequence for coherent or solid quasi-coherent cohomology. The classical Cousin complex (Hartshorne, Residues and Duality, IV), of which this is a variant, is not planned either. The paper applies the theorem in §4.5 (p. 52) to the stratification of the Siegel variety by length of Weyl elements.

items.name: Replacing a chain of maps of complexes by termwise split injections ([Sta22], Tag 014M)
items.statement: As used in the proof of Theorem 2.9.7: a finite chain of maps A_{d−1}^• → ⋯ → A_{−1}^• of bounded above complexes can be replaced, up to homotopy (by homotopy equivalent bounded above complexes), by a chain in which every map A_i^• → A_{i−1}^• is a termwise split injection.
items.note: Missing. Tag 014M is Lemma 13.9.15 of the Stacks Project, in the section 'Cones and termwise split sequences'. Let 𝒜 be an additive category and A₁ → ⋯ → A_n a sequence of composable maps of complexes. Then there is a commutative diagram with a chain B₁ → ⋯ → B_n of termwise split injections and homotopy equivalences B_i → A_i. If all the A_i are bounded above (resp. below, bounded), so are the B_i. Mathlib has the ingredients at the pinned commit but not this factorization. FoundationsAndLibraryIntegration LI.3 plans homological algebra only in general terms ('resolutions, derived functors, spectral sequences') and does not name this lemma. External input: The Stacks Project [Sta22], Tag 014M, as cited by the paper.

items.name: Spectral sequence of a filtered complex ([Sta22], Tag 012M)
items.statement: A complex K^• with a finite decreasing filtration by subcomplexes F^pK^• has a spectral sequence E₁^{p,q} = H^{p+q}(gr^p K^•) ⇒ H^{p+q}(K^•), which converges because the filtration is finite.
items.note:
Planned in FoundationsAndLibraryIntegration LI.3, 'Categories, homological algebra and sheaves', whose selected sources include the Stacks Project. Tag 012M is Stacks Lemma 12.24.2: a filtered complex has a spectral sequence (E_r, d_r)_{r≥0} with E₁^{p,q} = H^{p+q}(gr^p K^•). Convergence for a finite filtration is Lemma 12.24.11 of the same section: the spectral sequence is bounded and converges to H^*(K^•). Mathlib at the pinned commit has part of this (the declarations listed).
- The spectral sequence of a spectral object in an abelian category.
- The abelian spectral object obtained by applying a homological functor to a triangulated one.
- The spectral object of mapping cones in the homotopy category. Its documentation says it attaches a spectral object to any functor ι ⥤ CochainComplex C ℤ, for example a filtered complex.
Mathlib lacks the identification of the first page with H^{p+q}(gr^p) for filtered complexes, and the convergence. Its file on triangulated spectral objects records: 'the spectral sequence is already constructed: it remains to study convergence'. External input: The Stacks Project [Sta22], Tag 012M, as cited by the paper.

items.name: §2.9.8: a cohomological correspondence together with a filtration
items.statement: Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence (Definition 2.1.8): X and C are separated of finite type over S, p₁, p₂ : C ⇒ X, and p₁ × p₂ : C → X × X is proper. Let F ∈ D(𝒪_{X,■}). Let T : p₂^⋆F → p₁^!F be a cohomological correspondence, i.e. a map in D(𝒪_{C,■}). Let Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z₀ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ Z_d = X be a filtration of X by closed subschemes.
items.note:
Missing. The underlying objects are planned or available:
- D(𝒪_{C,■}), p₂^⋆ and p₁^! are part of AnalyticStacks AS.3's solid formalism;
- Mathlib has spans (CategoryTheory.Limits.span) and proper morphisms (AlgebraicGeometry.IsProper), so a span C ⇉ X with p₁ × p₂ proper can be expressed.
The notion of a cohomological correspondence p₂^⋆F → p₁^!F for coherent or solid quasi-coherent sheaves, with its action on cohomology, is planned nowhere. EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.8 plans it only for étale sheaves: 'Construct cohomological correspondences c₂* K→c₁^!K'. This is the solid-sheaf form of the adjoint description in Pilloni, Duke Math. J. 169 (2020), Remark 4.3.2 (maps p₂^*F → p₁^!G). That coherent notion is also unplanned and is proposed for the Part II of AutomorphicBundles named in the route.

items.name: The map of localization triangles induced by T when Z_l is contracted
items.statement:
In the setting of §2.9.8, fix l and assume p₁^{−1}(Z_l) ⊆ p₂^{−1}(Z_l) set-theoretically. Equivalently, C_{U_l,2} := p₂^{−1}(U_l) ⊆ C_{U_l,1} := p₁^{−1}(U_l); these are open subschemes of C, with open immersions j_{C_{U_l,k}} : C_{U_l,k} ↪ C. Then T extends to a map of exact triangles
from p₂^⋆(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F → p₂^⋆F → p₂^⋆(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆F →(+1)
to p₁^!(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F → p₁^!F → p₁^!(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆F →(+1),
with middle map T. The left map is the composite
p₂^⋆(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F = (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_!j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}}p₂^⋆F → (j_{C_{U_l,2}})_!j^⋆_{C_{U_l,2}}p₁^!F → (j_{C_{U_l,1}})_!j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}}p₁^!F → p₁^!(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F.
The equality is base change, the first arrow is induced by T, and the second comes from C_{U_l,2} ⊆ C_{U_l,1}. The last arrow is adjoint, under (p₁)_! ⊣ p₁^!, to (p₁)_!(j_{C_{U_l,1}})_!j^⋆_{C_{U_l,1}}p₁^!F = (j_l)_!(p′₁)_!(p′₁)^!(j_l)^!F → (j_l)_!(j_l)^!F = (j_l)_!j_l^⋆F. This is induced by the counit (p′₁)_!(p′₁)^! → Id for p′₁ = p₁| : C_{U_l,1} → U_l. The right map is induced on cones.

items.name: Proposition 2.9.9: T acts on the Cousin spectral sequence
items.statement:
Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) be a correspondence with p₁ proper. The paper leaves this hypothesis implicit [sourceIssues E42]; it holds in the application. Let F ∈ D(O_{X,■}), let T : p₂^⋆F → p₁^!F be a cohomological correspondence, and let Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z₀ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ Z_d = X be a filtration by closed subschemes. Assume that p₁^{−1}(Z_l) ⊆ p₂^{−1}(Z_l) set-theoretically for all 0 ≤ l ≤ d, i.e. every Z_l is contracted by the correspondence. Then:
(a) T induces endomorphisms of RΓ(Ẑ_l, F), RΓ_c(U_l, F) and RΓ_c(Ẑ_l ∖ Ẑ_{l−1}, F) for all 0 ≤ l ≤ d, compatible with the natural morphisms between them (the triangles of §2.9.5 and Lemma 2.9.6);
(b) if F ∈ D^−(O_{X,■}), the spectral sequence of Theorem 2.9.7 is T-equivariant.
For G one of the sheaves (j_l)_!j_l^⋆F, F, (î_l)_⋆î_l^⋆F, …, the endomorphism of RΓ(X, G) is the composite RΓ(X, G) → RΓ(C, p₂^⋆G) → RΓ(C, p₁^!G) → RΓ(X, G). The middle arrow is the corresponding vertical arrow of the map of exact triangles, with middle arrow T, constructed in the proof. It goes from p₂^⋆(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F → p₂^⋆F → p₂^⋆(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆F →(+1) to p₁^!(j_l)_!j_l^⋆F → p₁^!F → p₁^!(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆F →(+1). The last arrow is the trace RΓ(C, p₁^!G) = RΓ(X, (p₁)_!p₁^!G) → RΓ(X, G), which uses p₁ proper.

items.name: Cohomology with support RΓ_Z(Y, F) and RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F)
items.statement: Let Y → Spec A be a scheme (of finite type; A noetherian as in §2.1), let i : Z ↪ Y be a closed subscheme, and let F ∈ D(𝒪_{Y,■}). Put RΓ_Z(Y, F) := RΓ(Z, i^!F). Let î : Ẑ → Y be the corresponding closed subset of the locale, and put RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F) := RΓ(Ẑ, î^!F).
items.note:
Missing as a named notion, although the functors are planned.
- i^! for a closed immersion is the right adjoint of i_⋆ = i_! in AnalyticStacks AS.3's formalism, since closed immersions are proper.
- î^! is the right adjoint for the closed immersion of the locale. Rodríguez Camargo's Remark 5.1.5 (SolidAnalyticRings SA.2) gives î_⋆î^!M = Hom(R̂^I, M).
The two cohomologies differ. Take Y = Spec R, Z = Spec R/J with √J = √I, and M a discrete R-module:
- RΓ_Z computes Ext_R^•(R/J, M);
- RΓ_Ẑ is local cohomology, RΓ_{V(I)}(M) = colim_n RHom_R(R/I^n, M). This follows from the second localization triangle (checked by direct computation).
In that case the cohomology modules of RΓ_Ẑ are Mathlib's localCohomology I i, the colimit of Ext^i(R/I^t, M). Cohomology with supports is otherwise planned only for étale coefficients, in EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.0: 'Construct cohomology with support as the localization fiber, retaining the closed immersion'.

items.name: Lemma 2.10.1(1): the map RΓ_Z(Y, F) → RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F)
items.statement: In the setting of §2.10 (Y → Spec A, i : Z ↪ Y a closed subscheme, F ∈ D(𝒪_{Y,■})), there is a natural map RΓ_Z(Y, F) → RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F). It comes from the factorization i : Z →(u) Ẑ →(î) Y and the map u_⋆i^!F → î^!F adjoint to the identity i^!F → u^!î^!F.
items.note: Missing. It is formal once the planned functors of AnalyticStacks AS.3 and SolidAnalyticRings SA.2 exist. The map D(Z) → D(Ẑ) exists because R/J ⊗ R̂^I = R/J, so R/J-modules are R̂^I-modules.
