(1) Derived pullback preserves pseudo-coherence, and the solid pullback of a discrete object is the usual derived pullback, which is discrete. (2) For an invertible L, the projection formula for p̄^! follows formally: take right adjoints in p̄_!(G ⊗ p̄^*L^{-1}) ≅ p̄_!G ⊗ L^{-1}. (3) Discreteness of p̄^!F̄. First, f^! is local on the source ((f∘j)^! = j^*f^! for open j), so one may assume f : Spec B → Spec A is affine of finite type. Factor f as a closed immersion i into A^n_A followed by h : A^n_A → Spec A. Then h^! = h^*(−)[n] preserves discrete objects. For a closed immersion into Spec C with C noetherian, i^!N = RHom_C(B, N) is computed from a resolution of B by finite free C-modules. When N is discrete and bounded below (for example a coherent sheaf), this is a bounded-below complex in which each term is a finite sum of terms of N, so it is discrete. Clausen–Scholze (Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, Theorem 8.13(iv)) state only the case f^!A. Neither library has solid quasi-coherent sheaves: Mathlib has only the predicate CondensedMod.IsSolid on condensed modules. The draft roadmap AnalyticStacks covers part of the statement. AS.0 has 'the projection and base-change formulas they satisfy', which gives (2). AS.3 has 'maps of finite Tor-dimension are suave', which gives (3) when p̄ has finite Tor-dimension. No layer states (3) for a general proper map: AS.3 has only 'for proper f, f_* preserves pseudocoherent and coherent objects'.

items.name: Derived limits of essentially zero and Mittag-Leffler systems
items.statement: An essentially zero inverse system of modules has vanishing derived limit. For an inverse system (K_n)_n of complexes there is an exact sequence 0 → lim^1_n H^{i−1}(K_n) → H^i(lim_n K_n) → lim_n H^i(K_n) → 0. So if (H^{i−1}(K_n))_n satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition, then H^i(lim_n K_n) ≅ lim_n H^i(K_n). This holds for inverse systems of finite modules over an artinian ring.
items.note:
Used on p. 16 in the proof of Proposition 2.3.5: '{M[f^n]}_n is an essentially zero inverse system and so its limit is zero', and 'the system {H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n F̄)}_n satisfies the Mittag-Leffler property (since it is a system of finite A-modules), hence H^i(X̄, j_!F) = lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n F̄)'.

Planned in two layers.
- CompletedCohomologyPartII CC.2: 'Construct the derived inverse limit of complexes and the Milnor exact sequence; exhibit the possible lim¹ term rather than commuting completion and cohomology formally. Prove sufficient surjectivity/Mittag–Leffler criteria at each use.'
- DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra P7: 'Work with finite coefficient quotients before inverse limits, prove derived Mittag–Leffler comparisons, and retain lim¹ whenever it does not vanish.'

What the libraries have:
- Mathlib states the Mittag-Leffler condition only for Type-valued cofiltered systems (CategoryTheory.Functor.IsMittagLeffler).
- Neither library has lim¹ or the Milnor exact sequence.
- The Mittag-Leffler property of an inverse system of finite modules over an artinian ring follows from two Mathlib results, applied to the images of the transition maps: isArtinian_of_fg_of_artinian' (a finite module over an artinian ring is artinian) and IsArtinian.monotone_stabilizes (descending chains of submodules stabilise).

In the paper these limits are formed in solid modules. Countable products are exact there, so the same exact sequence holds, and evaluating at a point recovers the classical lim and lim¹ of the underlying modules.

items.name: Local solid computations: products and localizations
items.statement: Let A be a ring of finite type over Z and M̄ a pseudo-coherent object of D((A, A)■). Then M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} ∏_{n≥1} A = ∏_{n≥1} M̄; in particular M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} A((X^{-1}))/A[X] = M̄[[X^{-1}]]X^{-1} = ∏_{n≥1} M̄X^{-n}. For a discrete A-module M and f ∈ A, the usual tensor product M ⊗_A A[1/f] = colim(M →f M →f ⋯) is already solid, so it computes the solid base change to A[1/f].
items.locator: §2.3.1, proof of Proposition 2.3.2, p. 15; §2.3.7, proof of Proposition 2.3.8, p. 16
items.note:
These are two facts about solid modules, used as the local computations in Propositions 2.3.2 and 2.3.8.
- p. 15, proof of Proposition 2.3.2: 'Since M̄ is pseudo-coherent, we find that M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} A((X^{-1}))/A[X] = M̄ ⊗_{(A,A)■} A[[X^{-1}]]X^{-1} = ∏_{n≥1} M̄X^{-n}'.
- p. 16, proof of Proposition 2.3.8: 'We use that if M is discrete the (usual) tensor product M ⊗_A A[1/f] is solid in D(A[1/f]■)'.

Both are planned in the draft roadmap SolidAnalyticRings, which follows Rodríguez Camargo's Notes on solid geometry (arXiv:2603.03012v1).

First fact. SA.3 lists 'Theorem 5.3.2: for R of finite type over Z, R_□[S]=lim_nR[S_n], D(R_□) is the derived category of its heart, and ∏_N R is flat. Propositions 5.3.3, 5.3.7 and 5.3.12'.
- Proposition 5.3.7(4) of those notes is the flatness of ∏_N R. Its proof shows that M ⊗_{R□} ∏_N R = ∏_N M for finitely presented M.
- Remark 5.3.8 states M ⊗^L_{R□} ∏_N R = ∏_N M for every pseudo-compact M.
- A pseudo-coherent M̄ is a bounded above complex of finite free modules. Flatness lets one compute the tensor product termwise, and products are exact, so the formula follows.

Second fact. SA.2 plans analytic rings, 'a full subcategory D(A) ⊆ D(A▷) that is closed under limits and colimits'.
- A[1/f] is itself complete, so every discrete A[1/f]-module, being a colimit of copies of A[1/f], is complete.
- The solid tensor product with A[1/f] = colim(A →f A →f ⋯) commutes with this colimit.

The roadmap works in the light condensed setting, while the paper cites Clausen–Scholze's κ-condensed theory. Only countable products occur here, so the difference does not matter. Mathlib has only the predicate CondensedMod.IsSolid and no solid tensor product.

items.name: Maps from a pseudo-coherent complex into a colimit of uniformly bounded below complexes
items.statement: Let Y be a noetherian scheme, P ∈ D_qc(Y) pseudo-coherent, and (E_n) a filtered system in D_qc(Y) with all E_n in D^{≥a} for one fixed integer a. Then Hom(P, colim_n E_n) = colim_n Hom(P, E_n). Locally P may be replaced by a bounded complex of finite free modules in the relevant range of degrees, and RΓ(Y, −) commutes with filtered colimits of uniformly bounded below complexes.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Proposition 2.3.13, p. 17
items.note:
Used on p. 17 in the proof of Proposition 2.3.13: 'We deduce a map p̄⋆₂F̄ → colim_{n≥0} p̄!₁F̄(nD_C). Since p̄⋆₂F̄ is pseudo coherent, this map factors through a map p̄⋆₂F̄ → p̄!₁F̄(nD_C) for n large enough.'

Why the lower bound matters. On a noetherian scheme the compact objects are the perfect complexes, so for a pseudo-coherent object that is not perfect, Hom(P, −) need not commute with filtered colimits. This lemma supplies what the step needs. The uniform lower bound holds in the application: p̄₁ is proper and F̄ is coherent, so p̄!₁F̄ is bounded below with coherent cohomology, and twisting by the line bundles O(nD_C) does not change the bound.

Proof of the lemma.
- Let E ∈ D^{≥a}, and represent P locally by a bounded above complex of finite free modules.
- The long exact sequence for the stupid truncation gives Hom(P, E) = Hom(σ_{≥a−1}P, E), and σ_{≥a−1}P is perfect.
- The colimit of the E_n again lies in D^{≥a}.
- To globalise, RΓ on a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme commutes with filtered colimits. The paper cites this fact as [Sta22], Tag 01FF, for Corollary 2.3.9.

Neither library has pseudo-coherent complexes, D_qc of a scheme, or compact objects of derived categories. No atlas layer states the lemma. Pseudo-coherence over rings appears in DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra P7, whose node on perfect complexes has 'equivalently K is pseudo-coherent of finite Tor dimension'. AnalyticStacks AS.1 plans the formalism X ↦ D_qc(X) with the statement of Theorem 8.10 on pseudo-coherent objects. Neither plans this compactness statement.

items.name: Finiteness of Hom between bounded coherent complexes, and splitting of idempotents in D(A)
items.statement: Let A be a noetherian ring and M, N bounded complexes of finitely generated A-modules. Then Hom_{D(A)}(M, N) is a finitely generated A-module; in particular the A-subalgebra of End_{D(A)}(M) generated by one endomorphism T is a finite A-algebra. D(A) has countable direct sums, hence is idempotent complete (Bökstedt–Neeman). So every idempotent e of End_{D(A)}(M) splits, M ≅ eM ⊕ (1 − e)M.
items.locator: Used in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3, p. 18
items.note:
Used on p. 18 in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3: 'We consider the algebra B generated by T in End(M). This is a finite A-algebra. It splits into a product of local A-algebras, B = ∏_i B_i. We have idempotents e_i attached to each B_i and we let M_i = e_iM.' Here End(M) is taken in D(A), so two facts are needed: End_{D(A)}(M) is finite over A, and idempotents split in D(A). Lemma 2.4.3 is then used in Lemma 2.4.4(3) and Lemma 2.4.6 (p. 19) and in Proposition 2.5.4 (p. 20).

What the libraries have (partial only):
- Mathlib proves ModuleCat.finite_ext: Ext^i_R(N, M) is a finite R-module when R is noetherian and N, M are finite. The statement for bounded complexes follows by induction on the number of nonzero cohomology modules, using the truncation triangles and the fact that finite modules over a noetherian ring are closed under submodules, quotients and extensions.
- Mathlib has the notion CategoryTheory.IsIdempotentComplete, but no instance for derived categories.
- Neither library has the Bökstedt–Neeman theorem that a triangulated category with countable coproducts is idempotent complete.

What the atlas plans, for perfect complexes only:
- IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants IHG.2: 'For a Hecke action on a bounded perfect complex define its finite image algebras … Prove localization decompositions over complete coefficient rings, support and annihilator lemmas and finite generation'.
- DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra P9: 'localize this derived action by idempotents', for a perfect complex.

These layers do not cover Lemma 2.4.3. Its complexes, for example RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋)) in Proposition 2.5.4, are bounded complexes of finite modules over an artinian ring. They need not be perfect, because no flatness is assumed there.

items.name: Tor-independence of schemes over a base
items.statement: Morphisms X → S and S′ → S are Tor-independent if Tor_i^{O_{S,s}}(O_{X,x}, O_{S′,s′}) = 0 for all i > 0 and all points x ∈ X, s′ ∈ S′ lying over the same s ∈ S. Equivalently, the derived fibre product agrees with X ×_S S′, i.e. O_{X×_S S′} = O_X ⊗^L_{O_S} O_{S′}. This holds, for example, when X or S′ is flat over S.
items.locator: Used in §2.6.12 and the proof of Proposition 2.6.13, pp. 22–23 (also in the proof of Lemma 2.2.2, p. 12)
items.note:
Uses in the paper:
- p. 12, proof of Lemma 2.2.2: '(note that C̄ and X are tor-independent)'.
- p. 23, hypothesis of §2.6.12 and Proposition 2.6.13: 'We assume that X and S′ are tor independent and that F is A-flat'.
- p. 23, proof of Proposition 2.6.13, where the hypothesis is used in the form 'By tor independence O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′'.

The definition is the standard one (Stacks Project, Tag 08IA). The equivalence with the derived fibre product holds because Tor of the global rings localises to the Tor of local rings at pairs of points over the same point of S. Flatness of either morphism implies Tor-independence.

Mathlib has Tor functors in a monoidal abelian category with projective resolutions (CategoryTheory.Tor), which applies to modules over a commutative ring. Neither library defines Tor-independence of morphisms of schemes or compares the classical and derived fibre products. No atlas layer plans it: DerivedDeRhamCohomology DD.0 only warns that 'A pushout of ordinary rings without Tor independence is not a derived pushout'.

items.name: Products of copies of R are compact projective solid R-modules
items.statement: Let R be a ring of finite type over Z. For every set I, the product ∏_I R is a compact projective object of the category of solid R-modules (up to isomorphism it is the free solid R-module on a suitable profinite set) (Clausen–Scholze). Consequently every bounded complex whose terms are finite direct sums of such products is a compact object of D(R_■). In particular R̂^I is compact in D(R_■), since Lemma 2.9.2 represents it by a bounded complex with terms R^ℕ.
items.locator: proof of Lemma 2.9.2, p. 27; proof of Lemma 2.9.3, p. 28
items.note:
Used twice, and the paper gives no reference:
- p. 27, proof of Lemma 2.9.2: 'This implies that R̂^{(f₁,…,f_{r−1})} is a compact object in D(R■), represented by a bounded complex, whose terms are of the form R^ℕ'.
- p. 28, proof of Lemma 2.9.3: 'R̂^I is a compact object of D(R■)'.

These uses involve only countable products: R[[X]] ≅ ∏_ℕ R and its solid tensor powers.

Planned in the draft roadmap SolidAnalyticRings, in the light condensed setting.
- SA.1: '∏_N Z is a compact projective generator of Solid'.
- SA.3: 'Theorem 5.3.2: for R of finite type over Z, R_□[S]=lim_nR[S_n] … Propositions 5.3.3, 5.3.7 and 5.3.12'. Taking S = ℕ ∪ {∞} gives R_□[S] = ∏_ℕ R. The proof of Proposition 5.3.7 in Rodríguez Camargo's Notes on solid geometry begins 'The category Mod_{R□} has a compact projective generator given by ∏_N R'.

A bounded complex of compact objects is compact, which gives the consequence for R̂^I. The form for arbitrary index sets I is not planned; it belongs to Clausen–Scholze's κ-condensed theory, where the products ∏_I R are compact projective generators. The uses above need only ∏_ℕ R.

items.name: Hodge–Tate preimage of FL(Q_p) and the position of the Iwahori flag
items.statement: π^{-1}_{HT,K_{p,n}} of the image of FL(Q_p) in |FL|/K_{p,n} is the closure of the ordinary locus 𝒮^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},ord} of 𝒮^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}}. Over π_HT^{-1}(Pw), w ∈ ^MW, one has Lie_A(1) = ⟨e_{w^{-1}(i)} : g+1 ≤ i ≤ 2g⟩ under the trivialization of the Tate module, so these vectors span its multiplicative part. H_{g+i} corresponds to ⟨e_{g+1}, …, e_{g+i}⟩ mod p^n, because K_{p,n} stabilizes this flag mod p^n. Hence over π^{-1}_{HT,K_{p,n}}(w·K_{p,n}), Gr_{g+i} (1 ≤ i ≤ g) is multiplicative if g+i ∈ w^{-1}{g+1, …, 2g} and étale otherwise.
items.note: This item is kept for its first assertion. The paper uses it without proof or reference; the proof of Lemma 4.1.6 (p. 41) opens with 'We know that π^{-1}_{HT,K_{p,n}}(FL(Q_p)) = closure of 𝒮^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},ord}, is the closure of the ordinary locus.' The other assertions are the rest of that proof, which is already recorded with Lemma 4.1.6: Lie_A(1) = ⟨e_{w^{-1}(i)} : g+1 ≤ i ≤ 2g⟩ over π_HT^{-1}(Pw); H_{g+i} ↔ ⟨e_{g+1}, …, e_{g+i}⟩ mod p^n; and the type of each Gr_{g+i}. They were checked by direct computation with the convention w·e_i = e_{w(i)}, which matches w(diag(t)) = diag(t_{w^{-1}(1)}, …). With this convention w^{-1}⟨e_{g+1}, …, e_{2g}⟩ = ⟨e_{w^{-1}(i)} : i ≥ g+1⟩, and B (lower block triangular, with upper triangular diagonal blocks) stabilizes each ⟨e_{g+1}, …, e_{g+i}⟩. The external assertion links the Hodge–Tate period map to the ordinary locus of the Iwahori-level integral model, including its toroidal boundary. One proof goes through the classification of p-divisible groups over O_C by their Hodge–Tate filtration: the filtration Lie_A(1) ⊆ T_p(A) ⊗ C is Q_p-rational exactly when A[p^∞] is an extension of an étale group by a multiplicative one. At the boundary, the abelian part of the semi-abelian degeneration replaces A. No layer plans this. The atlas plans the Siegel Hodge–Tate map (PerfectoidShimuraVarieties S1, S3), but it plans Hodge–Tate fibres only for the unitary data of Caraiani–Scholze. IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentration IG.3 reads: 'For a geometric flag point x=Spa(C,O_C)→Fl, identify its polarized p-divisible group over O_C and special fiber X'. Neither library has p-divisible groups.

items.name: Degrees of truncated Barsotti–Tate groups and extreme values of the degree
items.statement: Let V be as in §4.2.7, with v(p) = 1. For a p-divisible group G over V, deg G[p^m] = m·dim G. A truncated Barsotti–Tate group of level n and dimension d has degree nd, in particular a multiple of n. For a finite flat group scheme H of order p^h, 0 ≤ deg H ≤ h. deg H = 0 iff H is étale, and deg H = h iff H is multiplicative, since deg H + deg H^D = h.
items.locator: proofs of Proposition 4.2.8 and Corollary 4.2.10, p. 45; proof of Proposition 4.2.14, p. 46
items.note: This item is kept: these basic properties of Fargues's degree are used without statement. The proof of Proposition 4.2.8 (p. 45) needs deg G[p] = dim G for 'H[p^l]/H[p^{l−1}] is a BT_1 of degree deg H[p] = dim G − deg L'. It needs the same fact, with additivity, for 'deg p^{-1}H = deg H + deg G[p], deg p^{-n}L = deg L + deg G[p^n]'. Corollary 4.2.10 (p. 45) concludes that the groups 'are BT_n's and their degree is a multiple of n'. Proposition 4.2.14 (p. 46) uses 'n ≥ deg p_2^*H_{g+1,x} ≥ deg p_1^*H_{g+1,x} ≥ 0' and reads off étale groups at degree 0 and multiplicative groups at degree n. The bounds 0 ≤ deg H ≤ h and the two extreme cases already follow from facts recorded with Fargues's divisor: D_H + D_{H^D} = V(p^h), and the complement of D_H is the étale locus. The new content is deg H = n·d for a truncated Barsotti–Tate group H of level n and dimension d, because ω_H is free of rank d over V/p^n. This includes deg G[p^m] = m·dim G. Neither library has p-divisible or truncated Barsotti–Tate groups; the library audit finds no p-divisible group in either. No layer plans Fargues's degree. The extraction of Pilloni (Duke 2020) routes the degree to HodgeTateAndCanonicalSubgroups T0 by a source route (definition, additivity, deg G + deg G^D = height, growth along generic isomorphisms), and BT_n to FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory R07.1.

items.name: Conjecture 5.6.1 for w = Id and w = w_0^M in every genus (Remarks 1.4.4 and 5.6.4)
items.statement: For every g ≥ 1, Conjecture 5.6.1 holds for w = Id and for w = w_0^M, the longest element of ^MW (Remark 1.4.4). Remark 5.6.4 says that the same kind of argument as in Proposition 5.6.3 would prove the expected vanishing of RΓ_w(K^p) or RΓ_w(K^p, cusp) for certain particular w and all g, but that the authors could not find a general argument.
items.locator: §5.6, Remark 5.6.4 and the case w = Id in the proof of Proposition 5.6.3, p. 58; Remark 1.4.4, p. 5
